The documents from the first century and first half of the second century are more focused on dealing with internal church matters and the teachings of Jesus and the apostles. However, starting in the mid-second century, we see the emergence of a distinct genre of Christian literature known as “apologies” or “apologetics.”

Apologists were Christian writers who sought to defend and explain the Christian faith to both non-Christians and Christians alike. Their writings often addressed criticisms and misconceptions about Christianity, as well as providing a rational basis for belief in Jesus Christ and the Christian message.

This lecture focused on the Desert Fathers and their approach to Christian mission. The Desert Fathers were early Christian hermits, ascetics, and monks who lived often in the deserts.

The list of apologists from the 2nd and 3rd centuries included:

Justin Martyr (c. 100–165 AD)

Quadratus (fl. c. 124–132 AD)

Aristides of Athens (c. 100–c. 165 AD)

Tatian (c. 120–c. 180 AD)

Melito of Sardis (fl. mid-2nd century AD)

Athenagoras of Athens (c. 133–c. 190 AD)

Theophilus of Antioch (c. 120–c. 190 AD)

Tertullian (c. 155–c. 240 AD)

Clement of Alexandria (c. 150–c. 215 AD)

Origen (c. 184–c. 253 AD)

This is list is not exhaustive, but it includes some of the most prominent figures who contributed to the development of Christian theology and defended the faith against various criticisms during this period.

The primary purposes of these apologies were:

To defend Christianity against accusations and misconceptions held by both pagan and Jewish critics. (defensive)

To advance the understanding of Christian beliefs and practices among non-Christians. (offensive)

To demonstrate the reasonableness and moral superiority of the Christian faith. (evangelistic)

To encourage and strengthen the faith of Christian believers in the face of persecution and societal pressure. (constructive)

Justin Martyr is one of the most well-known early Christian apologists. He wrote several works defending Christianity, including “First Apology” and “Second Apology.” In these writings, Justin addressed the Roman authorities and the general public, explaining Christian beliefs and practices while refuting common accusations against Christians, such as atheism and immorality.

Martyr welcomed classical philosophy, particularly Platonism, as a way to understand and articulate Christian doctrine. He believed that truth could be found in both Christian revelation and philosophical inquiry.

Martyr and Plato

Justin Martyr welcomed classical philosophy. He believed that Plato’s teaching on eternal forms referred to the God of the Bible, that Socrates, (like Abraham) was ‘a Christian before Christ’, and that Socrates’ death was an example for Christian martyrs.

He was a gentile born in Samaria, converted to Christianity, and was eventually martyred for his faith. He was trained in Greek philosophy before his conversion. Martyr moved to Rome after his conversion, where he established a Christian school and engaged in public debates with pagan philosophers.

His work in the “First Apology” focus on the connection between the Old Testament and Jesus as the Messiah, arguing that Christianity was the fulfillment of Jewish prophecy. He also addressed ethical teachings, emphasizing the moral superiority of Christian living compared to pagan practices.

📚 Further Reading on Justin Martyr

Chapter 7 of 

Gonzalez (2010) provides a good overview of the context of the desert fathers’ lives and works.

As we started talking about this document, we discussed about the fact that the canon was still not closed in the early second century. This will be discussed later, but it is important to note that most of these documents were considered scripture by some early Christian communities.

The 

Epistle of Barnabas is an early Christian writing that was likely composed in the late first or early second century. It is attributed to Barnabas, a companion of the Apostle Paul, although the true authorship is uncertain. The epistle addresses various theological themes, including the relationship between Judaism and Christianity, the interpretation of Old Testament scriptures, and the ethical conduct expected of Christians. The Epistle of Barnabas emphasizes the idea that Christians are the true heirs of God’s covenant, interpreting Old Testament laws in a spiritualized manner.

The letter known as 

1 Clement is attributed to Clement of Rome, who was a prominent leader in the early Christian community in Rome. The letter was written to the church in Corinth around 99 AD, addressing a dispute that had arisen within the Corinthian church regarding leadership and authority. This letter contains the same substance as Paul’s letters, emphasizing humility, unity, and obedience to church leaders.

The Didache, an early Christian text that provides insight into the beliefs and practices of the Apostolic Fathers. Apparently, there were found one original fragment and one copy, both in Greek. 

Source

The 

Didache, also known as “The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles,” is an early Christian document that provides instructions on various aspects of Christian life and practice. It was written in the late first or early second century. It covers topics such as baptism, fasting, prayer, the Eucharist, and church organization. The Didache reflects the communal and ethical dimensions of early Christian life, emphasizing the importance of living according to the teachings of Jesus and the apostles.

The first part of the Didache focuses on ethical teachings, including the “Two Ways” doctrine, which contrasts the way of life (following God’s commandments) with the way of death (sinful behavior). The second part provides practical instructions for Christian rituals and community life.

Aspects of the church life in the Didache

Ransom was a big topic for the early church. Also, abundance grace is seen in the Didache, to the point that those cathecumens will observe baptized Christians’ generosity after participating in the Eucharist.

New Christians were invited to participate of the cathechumenate, a period of learning and preparation before baptism. After baptism, they would be fully integrated into the Christian community, participating in communal meals and the Eucharist. This was normally done during lent, every day. Christians were expected to participate in the teaching of the discipleship with their guests. Questions would be asked to the teachers, and the teachers would provide answers based on the teachings of Jesus and the apostles. Baptism was done in Easter.

The last document discussed in class was The Shepherd of Hermas. This was very close to be included in the New Testament canon, but it was ultimately not accepted as scripture. Its text is a call to shape life according to what a Christian life should look like.

Questions such as “Can you repent of major sins after baptism?” and others are part of the struggles of the early church. Disagreements are part of the life of the church, but the greater concern is to be formed into Jesus form. This document will touch on these themes.

The 

The Shepherd of Hermas is an early Christian literary work that was likely written in the mid-second century. It is a visionary text that combines elements of apocalyptic literature, moral exhortation, and allegory. The work is presented as a series of visions and parables experienced by a Christian named Hermas, who is guided by a figure known as the Shepherd. The Shepherd of Hermas addresses themes such as repentance, forgiveness, and the importance of living a virtuous life. It also reflects the challenges faced by the early Christian community, including issues of sin, discipline, and the hope for ultimate salvation.

The following documents were not discussed in class but are part of the Apostolic Fathers literature and were mentioned. We were also asked to read the Letters to the Magnesians, Romans, and Smyrnaeans from Ignatius of Antioch as preparation for the studies on the martyrs of the early church.

Translated by J. B. Lightfoot.

Ignatius of Antioch was an early Christian bishop who wrote a series of letters to various Christian communities while on his way to Rome for martyrdom around 110 AD. His letters emphasize the importance of church unity, the role of bishops, and the significance of the Eucharist. Ignatius strongly advocated for obedience to church leaders and warned against divisions within the Christian community. He also highlighted the reality of persecution and the need for Christians to remain faithful in the face of suffering.

Hymn 314 from Genevan Psalter

The lecture started with the Hymn 314 from Genevan Psalter.

Very little is known about the period between the New Testament writings and the early second century. However, we do have some writings from early Christian leaders known as the Apostolic Fathers. These writings provide valuable insights into the beliefs, practices, and challenges faced by the early Christian community during this formative period.

Some of the main sources from the Apostolic Fathers include:

1 Clement

Didache

Ignatius of Antioch’s 7 Letters

Epistle of Barnabas

The Shepherd of Hermas (ca. 90-150)

What does this literature tell us how early Christians (90-150 AD) perceived their mission in Hellenistic culture?

Hellenistic culture

The Hellenistic culture, which emerged after the conquests of Alexander the Great, was characterized by the spread of Greek language, art, architecture, and philosophy throughout the Mediterranean and Near Eastern regions. This cultural milieu significantly influenced the development of early Christianity, as it provided a common language (Koine Greek) and a rich intellectual tradition that early Christians engaged with in their theological reflections and missionary efforts.

Before touching on the Roman persecution of Christians, it is important to understand the context of the early church and one of its first major challenges: the question of Gentile converts and their relationship to Jewish customs. That is to say that persecution was not the only challenge the early church faced.

Acts 15 describes the first church council, which took place in Jerusalem around 50 AD. The council was convened to address the question of whether Gentile converts to Christianity needed to follow Jewish customs and laws, such as circumcision and dietary restrictions. The council ultimately decided that Gentile converts did not need to follow these customs, but they were asked to abstain from certain practices that were particularly offensive to Jewish Christians, such as eating food sacrificed to idols.

The meeting of the council was significant because it marked a turning point in the early church’s understanding of its identity and mission. It affirmed that Christianity was not simply a sect of Judaism but a distinct faith that welcomed Gentile believers. This decision helped to pave the way for the spread of Christianity throughout the Roman Empire and beyond.

It is quite fascinating that they wrote down the decisions of the council in a letter to be sent to the churches. This shows the importance of communication and unity in the early church, as well as the recognition that the decisions made at the council had implications for the wider Christian community.

The letter to the gentiles from Acts 15

28 It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us not to burden you with anything beyond the following requirements:

29 You are to abstain from food sacrificed to idols, from blood, from the meat of strangled animals and from sexual immorality. You will do well to avoid these things.

Farewell.

Fledging (early) Christians were called to make disciples who make disciples in this challenging context. The mission of the church was to proclaim the gospel and to live out the teachings of Jesus in a way that was faithful to their identity as followers of Christ.

The life of Christians in this period was marked by persecution and suffering, as they faced hostility from both the Roman authorities and the surrounding culture. The main figures of this period were:

Apostolic Fathers: Early Christian writers who were direct disciples of the apostles, such as Clement of Rome, Ignatius of Antioch, and Polycarp of Smyrna. They provided guidance and encouragement to the early Christian communities.

Martyrs: Christians who were persecuted and killed for their faith, such as Stephen, Perpetua, and Felicity. Their witness and sacrifice inspired others to remain faithful in the face of persecution.

Apologists: Christian writers who defended the faith against pagan criticisms and misconceptions, such as Justin Martyr and Tertullian. They sought to explain and justify Christian beliefs and practices in a way that was understandable to the broader culture.

Monks: Although monasticism would develop more fully in later centuries, some early forms of asceticism and communal living can be traced back to this period. Early ascetics sought to live lives of holiness and devotion, often withdrawing from the world to focus on prayer and spiritual discipline.

And that’s where we will pick up in the next lecture!

To understand the period from 100-313 AD, we need to understand the context of the Roman Empire during this time. The empire was vast and diverse, encompassing many different cultures and religions. The Roman government was generally tolerant of different religious practices, as long as they did not threaten the stability of the empire. However, Christians were often viewed with suspicion and hostility by the Roman authorities.

Politically, there is unity and peace in the Roman Empire. No major wars were happening for the last 200 years. This period is known as the Pax Romana, or Roman Peace. The empire was ruled by a series of emperors who maintained order and stability throughout the empire. The mentality that trusting in the goodness of human beings brought the hope of a permanent social order.

The Roman ideal became part of the cultural fabric of the empire. The emperor was seen as a divine figure, and loyalty to the empire was considered a civic duty. This created a challenging environment for Christians, who refused to worship the emperor or participate in certain civic rituals that were seen as idolatrous.

Culturally, the unified language, cultural uniformity, art, education (paideia), transportation, and communication networks helped to create a sense of shared identity and purpose among the diverse peoples of the empire.

Paideia

The Greek word “paideia” refers to the system of education and cultural upbringing in ancient Greece and Rome. It encompassed not only formal education but also the broader cultural values, norms, and practices that shaped individuals into well-rounded citizens. Paideia emphasized the development of intellectual, moral, and physical virtues, aiming to cultivate individuals who could contribute positively to society. In the Roman context, paideia included the study of literature, philosophy, rhetoric, and the arts, as well as physical training and civic responsibility.

Despite the general peace and stability of the Roman Empire during this period, the decadence of morality and the increasing use of Latin as the common language in the western part of the empire were signs of decline.

The moral decline of the Roman Empire is certainly connected to the religious situation, where a polytheistic and syncretistic approach to religion prevailed, leading to moral decay and spiritual emptiness. Also, there were two Roman Empires. The one worshiped by the people and the one that actually ruled. The intelligentsia was mostly skeptical of the traditional Roman religion and used it in a utilitarian way.

What is true?

Pontius Pilate posture when interrogating Jesus is a good representation of the Roman attitude towards religion: “What is truth?” (John 18:38). This question reflects the relativistic and pragmatic approach to religion that characterized the Roman Empire during this period.

Another characteristic of the Roman context is that life was cheap. The widespread acceptance of practices such as gladiatorial games, public executions, and other forms of entertainment that involved violence and death reflected a culture that devalued human life. This moral climate created a challenging environment for Christians, who were called to uphold the sanctity of life and reject the prevailing cultural norms.

Ambrose of Milan (c. 340-397 A.D.) was a Roman governor who became the Bishop of Milan and one of the most influential church leaders of the 4th century. Known for his eloquence, theological insight, and strong leadership, Ambrose played a crucial role in shaping the early Christian Church.



The Emperor Theodosius is forbidden by Saint Ambrose to enter Milan Cathedral. Anthony van Dyck, 1635-1640. 

Source

While governor, Ambrose was unexpectedly elected bishop by popular acclaim, despite being a catechumen (a person preparing for baptism). He embraced his new role with dedication and zeal. He went to the church in order to help calming down Arians and ortodox who wanted the next bishop to be one of their own. After a child cried out “Ambrose, bishop!” the people took it as a divine sign and tried to electe him on the spot. Ambrose failed successfully in his attempts to flee from the city. After the emperor showed his approval, Ambrose accepted the position and was baptized, ordained, and consecrated as bishop within a week.

Ambrose sought to devote himself fully to his episcopal duties. He was known for his strong stance against Arianism, popularizing the works of the Cappadocian Fathers in the West, and his efforts to promote Nicene Christianity.

He became a small babe so that you could be fully grown, perfect human beings; he was wrapped in swaddling clothes so that you might be freed from the bonds of death; he came to the manger to bring you to the altar; he was on earth so you might be in heaven. Commentary on Luke 2.41

After the invasion of Rome by the Goths in 410, Ambrose requested that the golden vessels of the church would be melted down to pay the ransom for the captives taken by the invaders. The criticism he received-mainly by the Arians’ party-for this act of charity did not deter him. He famously responded that the church’s treasures were meant to help people, not to adorn buildings.

Ambrose had a significant influence on 

Augustine of Hippo, one of the most important theologians in Christian history. Ambrose’s preaching and writings helped shape Augustine’s understanding of Christian doctrine and spirituality. In 387 A.D., Ambrose baptized Augustine in Milan, marking a pivotal moment in Augustine’s spiritual journey.



Massacre in the Hippodrome of Thessaloniki in 390, 16th-century wood engraving. 

Source

But the most famous event of Ambrose’s episcopate was his confrontation with Emperor Theodosius I after the massacre of Thessalonica in 390 A.D. One source tells that a Roman general was lynched in an urban riot after arresting a popular charioteer. In retaliation, Theodosius ordered his troops to massacre thousands of citizens in Thessalonica. When Theodosius came to Milan, Ambrose refused to allow him to enter the church until he did public penance for his actions. This bold stance by Ambrose demonstrated the growing power and influence of the Church in relation to the state.

In this section, we will explore the lives and contributions of Athanasius of Alexandria and the Cappadocian Fathers, who were instrumental in defending and developing the Nicene faith during the 4th century. Part of the context of their work was the 

Arian controversy, which challenged the orthodox understanding of the nature of Christ and the Trinity.

The results of the incarnation of the Savior are such and so many, that anyone attempting to enumerate them should be compared to a person looking upon the vastness of the sea and trying to count its waves. — Athanasius



Icon of Saint Athanasios, Antivouniotissa Museum, Kerkyra 

Source

Athanasius was the Bishop of Alexandria and one of the most important theologians of the early Christian church. He is best known for his staunch defense of the Nicene Creed against Arianism, which denied the full divinity of Jesus Christ.

Athanasius was a young man when he attended the 

Council of Nicaea in 325 AD as a deacon. He was so dark and short that his enemies called him “the black dwarf”. He became bishop of Alexandria in 328 AD and served in that role for over four decades, during which he faced multiple exiles due to his opposition to Arianism.

His origin is unknown, but he was likely born in Alexandria, Egypt and was possibly a Coptic. He would constantly be in contact with the monastic communities in the desert around Alexandria, which influenced his spirituality and theology. They would later offer him refuge during his exiles.

Gonzalez (2010, pg. 200) will attribute Athanasius’ theological brilliance to his close relationship with the desert monks and his monastic discipline, his roots among the people of Alexandria, and his deep study of Scripture.

Athanasius’ most famous work is “On the Incarnation,” in which he articulates the orthodox understanding of the incarnation of Christ. He argued that Jesus Christ is both fully God and fully human, and that through his incarnation, death, and resurrection, humanity is offered salvation and reconciliation with God. This work is even prior to his controversy with the Arians 

Gonzalez, 2010.

Arius taught that Jesus, the Son of God, was not truly God, but a lesser being, a creature. According to Arius, there was a time when the Son did not exist, and he was created by God the Father. This view challenged the orthodox understanding of the Trinity, which holds that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are co-eternal and of the same substance (homoousios).

As a result of the Arianism controversy, many monks left the cities to keep a pure faith in Jesus incarnate God.

Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, wanted Athanasius to be his successor. When Alexander died in 328, Athanasius was elected bishop. But before his death, Athanasius had withdrawn to the desert in order to keep his quiet life. There was no escape. As bishop, Athanasius continued to oppose Arianism and defend the Nicene faith. He faced significant opposition from Arian sympathizers and was exiled multiple times by various Roman emperors who supported Arianism. In the same year he became bishop, Constantine revoked his sentence exiling Arius.

Eusebius of Nicomedia, an Arian bishop, convinced Constantine to exile Athanasius under some lies. He was exiled to Trier in 335 AD. He would return to Alexandria in 337 after Constantine’s death.

Eusebius of Nicomedia would baptize Constantine on his deathbed in 337 AD, which further solidified Arian influence in the empire. His sons, Constantius II, Constantius, and Constans, would allow exiled bishops to return to their churches.

Athanasius was exiled again after a certain Gregory, a rival, convinced the governor that Athanasius was not legitimate bishop. As he tried to steal the churches from Athanasius, the situation escalated, and Athanasius saw himself forced to flee again to the desert. He would smuggle himself to Rome in 339 AD, where he was welcomed by Pope Julius I.

His time in Rome was fruitful, as he was able to gather support for the Nicene faith. Pope Julius I convened a synod that affirmed Athanasius’ position as the legitimate bishop of Alexandria and condemned Arianism and treated Gregory as an usurper.

After the death of Constantine II, the two other brothers agreed to allow Athanasius to return to Alexandria. He was received with great joy by the people. For ten years he would lead the church in Alexandria, strengthening the Nicene faith and combating Arianism.

Still, there was a problem: Emperor Constantius was an Arian sympathizer. He would endures Athanasius’ presence in Alexandria due to his brother’s insistence. He needed his brother’s support against the usurper Magnentius. In 353 A.D., Constantius felt strong enough to exile Athanasius again. This time, Athanasius fled to the desert monks, who hid him for five years and would transfer him from one monastery to another whenever officers of the empire would approach Athanasius’ hideout.

After Constantius’ unexpected death, Athanasius was able to return to Alexandria once more. The new emeperor, Julian, was not interested in Christian affairs and wanted to restore paganism. Athanasius would remain in Alexandria until his death in 373 AD.

To talk about the Capaddocian Fathers we need to start with a woman. Macrina the Younger was the sister of Basil the Great and Gregory of Nyssa. She was an ascetic and spiritual teacher who had a profound influence on her brothers and the development of monasticism in the Eastern Church. Later, Gregory of Nazianzus would also join this group of theologians that defended the Nicene faith and developed the doctrine of the Trinity.

Macrina was born around 324 AD in Caesarea, Cappadocia (modern-day Turkey). She came from a devout Christian family and was known for her piety and ascetic lifestyle. After the death of her parents, Macrina chose to live a life of celibacy and devotion to God. She established a monastic community for women, which became a model for Christian monasticism in the East.



Icon of Saint Macrina the Younger

Macrina had a great influence on the lives of her brothers. Basil the Great, after receiving his education in Constantinople and Athens, returned home and was a bostful and prideful man. Macrina confronted him about his arrogance and led him to embrace a life of humility and service. She also influenced Gregory of Nyssa, who would later write about her, highlighting her virtues and spiritual wisdom.

In her deathbed conversation with Gregory of Nyssa, Macrina articulated a profound understanding of the resurrection and the Christian hope in eternal life. Her teachings and example had a lasting impact on her brothers and the broader Christian community. This conversation is recorded in Gregory’s work 

“On the Soul and the Resurrection.”



The Cappadocian Fathers: Basil the Great, Gregory of Nazianzus, and Gregory of Nyssa

Important

Gregory of Nyssa was born around 335 AD in Caesarea, Cappadocia. He was the younger brother of Basil the Great and a close friend of Gregory of Nazianzus. Gregory had a very different personality from his brother Basil. He was more contemplative and mystical in his approach to theology.

He married a woman named Theosebia, who was also deeply involved in the Christian faith. After her death, Gregory decided to pursue a monastic life and was ordained a bishop. He became the bishop of Nyssa, a small town in Cappadocia. His writings reflect his life style, focusing on the mystical and spiritual aspects of the Christian faith.

He became a bishop ordained by his brother Basil. After the death of Valens and Basil, he became one of the leading defenders of Nicene orthodoxy. He participated in the 

Council of Constantinople in 381 AD, and was requested to travel throughout the Empire by Theodosius I to combat 

Arianism.

Basil the Great was born around 329 AD in Caesarea, Cappadocia. He came from a wealthy and influential Christian family. Basil received a classical education in Constantinople and Athens, where he studied rhetoric, philosophy, and theology. After completing his studies, Basil returned to Cappadocia. 

Gonzalez (2010, pg. 210) notes that Basil was “puffed up with his own wisdom” as he soon got a position teaching rhetoric in Caesarea. When his brother Naucratius passed unexpectedly, Basil was deeply affected and began to reconsider his life. Influenced by his sister Macrina, he decided to resign and started his journey learning the “secrets of religious life” and to live a monastic life.

Gregory of Nazianzus was Basil’s close friend from their studies in Athens. They shared a deep commitment to the Christian faith. They also founded a community of monks for men close to Annesi, in the same model as Macrina’s community for women.

Basil was later ordained a presbyter against his will. After some conflict with the bishop of Caesarea, Basil returned to his monastic community. Later, when Arianism resurged in Cappadocia, Basil was invited to join forces with the bishop of Caesarea to defend the Nicene faith.

In his return to Caesarea, Basil faced a dramatic situation. The crops were destroyed by the bad weather, and rich people were hoarding food to sell it at high prices. Basil organized the distribution of food to the poor and established a system of charity in the outskirts of the city. This system included a hospital, an almshouse, and a hospice for travelers. This complex was known as the Basiliad.

In one of his writings (“Homily on Luke’s Works”), Basil express his views on social justice and the responsibility of Christians to care for the poor:

If one who takes the clothing off another is called a thief, why give any other name to one who can clothe the naked and refuses to do so? The bread that you withhold belongs to the poor; the cape that you hide in your chest belongs to the naked; the shoes rotting in your house belong to those who must go unshod.

Basil was elected the bishop of Caesarea in 370 AD. After his election, the Arian emperor Valens prepared a visit to Caesarea, intending to overthrow Basil. However, Basil’s strong leadership and the support of the people prevented Valens from carrying out his plan. After being threatened to have his goods confiscated, exile, torture, or death, Basil boldly confronted Valens:

All that I have that you can confiscate are these rags and a few books. Nor can you exile me, for wherever you send me, I shall be God’s guest. As to torture you should know that my body is already dead in Christ. And death would be a great boon to me, leading me sooner to God.

He passed away a few months before the 

Council of Constantinople in 381 AD, which would further affirm the Nicene faith and condemn Arianism.

Gregory of Nazianzus was born around 329 AD in Arianzus, near Nazianzus, Cappadocia. He came from a devout Christian family and was a close friend of Basil the Great. Gregory received a classical education in Constantinople and Athens, where he studied rhetoric and philosophy. After completing his studies, Gregory returned to Cappadocia and became a teacher of rhetoric in Nazianzus.

Gregory was ordained a presbyter against his will. He tried to avoid getting leadership positions as he wanted to pursue a contemplative life. To his dismay, later Basil made him bishop of Sasima, a small town in Cappadocia. This act caused a rift between the two friends, as Gregory felt that Basil had forced him into a position he did not want. They never reconciled.

In 379 AD, Gregory was called to Constantinople. In 380 AD, the new Emperor Theodosius I, a Nicene Christian, ordained Gregory to become the Archbishop of Constantinople. Gregory reluctantly accepted the position but had no way to escape.

Gregory was meant to preside the Council of Constantinople in 381 AD. However, his opponents pointed out that he was already a bishop in Sasima, and thus could not preside over the council. Gregory resigned from his position as Archbishop of Constantinople and retired to a monastery in Nazianzus, where he spent the rest of his life writing theological works and sermons.

The Council of Constantinople in 381 AD was a significant event in the history of Christianity. It was convened by Emperor Theodosius I to address ongoing theological disputes, particularly the Arian controversy. The council reaffirmed the 

Nicene Creed and expanded it to include a more detailed description of the Holy Spirit’s divinity. It also condemned various heresies, including Arianism, Apollinarianism, and Macedonianism.

Augustine of Hippo (354-430 A.D.) was one of the most influential theologians and philosophers in Christian history. Born in Thagaste (modern-day Algeria), Augustine’s early life was marked by a search for truth, which eventually led him to embrace Christianity. His conversion experience in 386 A.D., as recounted in his autobiographical work Confessions, is one of the most famous spiritual journeys in Christian literature.

His main conversion event took place in a garden in Milan, where he heard a child’s voice chanting “take and read.” Interpreting this as a divine command, he opened the Bible to Romans 13:13-14, which led to his profound spiritual transformation.

Augustine was a manichaeist for almost a decade before converting to Christianity under the influence of his mother, Monica, and the preaching of 

Ambrose of Milan. After his conversion, Augustine was baptized by 

Ambrose in 387 A.D. He later returned to North Africa, where he was ordained a priest in 391 A.D. and became the Bishop of Hippo in 395 A.D.

Augustine’s theological contributions are vast and varied. He is perhaps best known for his works on original sin, grace, and the nature of the church. His writings, including The City of God and On Christian Doctrine, have had a lasting impact on Christian theology and Western philosophy.

Augustine faced mainly three significant heresies during his lifetime: Manichaeism, Donatism, and Pelagianism. He wrote extensively against these heresies, defending orthodox Christian doctrine and shaping the church’s understanding of key theological concepts.

Augustine’s early involvement with Manichaeism, a dualistic religion that posited a cosmic struggle between good and evil, deeply influenced his later theological reflections. After his conversion to Christianity, Augustine wrote Confessions, where he detailed his journey away from Manichaeism and towards Christian faith. He critiqued Manichaean beliefs, particularly their views on the nature of evil and the material world, arguing instead for a Christian understanding of creation and the problem of sin.

For Augustine, evil was not a substance or force in opposition to good, as the Manichaeans claimed, but rather a privation of good—a corruption of what is inherently good. This perspective laid the groundwork for his later theological explorations on sin and grace. According to Augustine, human will is weakened by original sin, and only through God’s grace can individuals be restored to righteousness. He used the concept of disordered love to explain how humans often misdirect their affections towards lesser goods, leading to sin.

In summary, evil is temporary and its origin is in the human will.

Donatism was a schism that arose in North Africa, centered around the issue of the sanctity of the church and its ministers. Donatists argued that clergy who had lapsed in faith during persecution could not validly administer sacraments. Augustine vehemently opposed this view, asserting that the efficacy of the sacraments did not depend on the moral purity of the minister but on the grace of God.

Augustine’s arguments against Donatism emphasized the unity of the church and the importance of forgiveness and reconciliation. He contended that the church is a mixed body of saints and sinners, and that God’s grace operates through the sacraments regardless of the personal holiness of the clergy. Augustine’s efforts were instrumental in suppressing the Donatist movement and reaffirming the catholic understanding of the church.

In summary, church looks more like ‘wheat and tares’ instead of ‘pure bride’, and sacraments are given by Christ, not the priest.

Pelagianism, named after the British monk Pelagius, was a theological doctrine that denied the concept of original sin and asserted that human beings could achieve salvation through their own efforts without the need for divine grace. Augustine strongly opposed Pelagianism, arguing that it undermined the necessity of God’s grace for salvation. He maintained that all humans inherit original sin from Adam, which corrupts human nature and renders individuals incapable of choosing good without God’s intervention. Augustine’s writings against Pelagianism, particularly in his work On the Grace of Christ and Original Sin, were crucial in shaping the church’s doctrine on grace and human nature.

Pelagianism starting point was the belief in the inherent goodness of human nature and the capacity for moral perfection through free will. Augustine countered this by emphasizing the total depravity of human nature due to original sin and the indispensable role of divine grace in enabling humans to turn towards God and achieve salvation. Augustine was also concerned that Pelagianism led people to be disheartened when they failed to live up to moral standards, as it placed the burden of salvation entirely on human effort.

In summary, sin is not the primary result of bad habits and social conditioning which people can overcome and grow to full adulthood. The original sin and the corruption make us as infants who are dependent on God’s grace.

11th-century conch mosaic of John Chrysostom from the south-east apse of the nave of the Hosios Loukas monastery

John Chrysostom, whose name means “Golden Mouth” in Greek, was one of the most renowned early Church Fathers and preachers. Born around 347 AD in Antioch, he became famous for his eloquent sermons and writings that emphasized moral reform and social justice. He was in essence a monk turned priest turned bishop.

Anthusa, John’s mother, was a devout Christian who played a significant role in his early religious education. She ensured that he received a solid foundation in Christian teachings and values. She was glad to hear that John wanted to be baptized when he was about 20 years old. She wasn’t so joyful when he decided to become a monk shortly after that and made him promise to wait until after her death.

To solve the domestic problem, John made his house into a monastery, and lived there as a monk with a few friends. They practiced extreme asceticism, including fasting and vigils. After his mother’s death, John went to the Syrian mountais to learn the disciplines of the monastic life. He spent four years learning, and then two more years in seclusion, living in a cave.

After his time in the desert, John returned to Antioch and was ordained a deacon and then a presbyter short after. He quickly gained a reputation for his powerful preaching and deep commitment to social justice. His sermons often addressed issues such as poverty, corruption, and the moral decay of society.

In 397 AD the bishopric of Constantinople became vacant, and John was chosen to fill the position. To not cause a riot in Antioch, he was kidnapped and taken to Constantinople, where he was consacrated in 398 AD. As bishop, he continued his preaching and social reform efforts, often clashing with the wealthy and powerful elite of the city. He was particularly critical of the excesses of the imperial court and the moral laxity of the clergy.

Among his reform efforts, John ordered:

that the “spiritual sisters” move out of the priests’ homes (a scandal at the time)

that priests live an austere life

that church finances be managed more transparently

that the luxurious items adorning the churches be sold to help the poor

that the clergy would open the doors at all hours to permit that workers and the poor to enter and receive assistance

His clashes with the imperial family, particularly Empress Eudoxia, led to his eventual exile in 403 AD. He was accused of various charges, including insubordination and heresy, and was forced to leave Constantinople. He died in exile in 407 AD.

Eudoxia felt like Chrysostom’s preachings fitted her like a glove. She didn’t like the eyes of the people turning to her as the example of luxury and excess that Chrysostom condemned. She then plotted to get rid of him raising false accusations against him.

John decided to leave the city in peace, to avoid a civil war. On the day of his departure, a massive earthquake struck Constantinople, which many saw as a divine sign of displeasure at John’s exile. Despite this, John was sent away. Fearing the wrath of God, Eudoxia later called him back.

Later, Chrysostom was exiled again to a remote location in the Cucusus. This time, the violence was greater, and many of his followers were tortured and exiled too.

The Bishop of Rome, Innocent I, protested strongly against the treatment of Chrysostom, but to no avail. John Chrysostom died in exile in 407 AD after being expelled from Cucusus.



One of the four so-claimed skull Reliquary of St. John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Constantinople.

Before he died, he preached his shortest sermon, saying, “Glory be to God for all things. Amen.”

Constantine the Great (c. 272-337 A.D.) was a Roman Emperor who played a crucial role in the history of Christianity. His conversion to Christianity and subsequent policies had a profound impact on the Christian church and its relationship with the Roman Empire. He got converted to Christianity in 312 A.D. after the Battle of the Milvian Bridge, where he reportedly saw a vision of the Christian cross and heard the words “In this sign, conquer.”



Modern bronze statue of Constantine I in York, England, near the spot where he was proclaimed Augustus in 306. 

Source

After his conversion, Constantine issued the Edict of Milan in 313 A.D., which granted religious tolerance to Christians and allowed them to practice their faith openly without fear of persecution. This marked a significant turning point for Christianity, as it transitioned from a persecuted minority religion to a favored and eventually dominant religion within the Roman Empire.

In 380 A.D., Emperor Theodosius I declared Christianity the official state religion of the Roman Empire with the Edict of Thessalonica. This further solidified the position of Christianity within the empire and led to the suppression of pagan practices.

The conversion of Constantine and the subsequent adoption of Christianity as the state religion had several significant effects on the Christian church:

Christians moved from the margins to becoming the religion of the state. From margins to the centre of culture.

Christians moved from a weak and persecuted minority to a powerful institution with political influence. From poor and humble places of worship to grand basilicas funded by the empire.

Christians moved from illegal gatherings in homes and catacombs to public worship and state-sponsored events. From secret meetings to public processions and ceremonies.

Christians moved from 

paroikoi (sojourners) to citizens of the empire with legal rights and privileges. From outsiders to insiders.

Constantine’s conversion and policies laid the foundation for the Christian church’s growth and influence in the centuries that followed. The church became intertwined with the state, leading to both opportunities and challenges for Christianity. While the church gained political power and resources, it also faced the risk of becoming too closely aligned with secular authorities.

His motives for converting to Christianity are still debated among historians. Some argue that he genuinely embraced the faith, while others suggest that his conversion was a strategic move to unify the empire under a single religion. Regardless of his motives, Constantine’s impact on the Christian church and its history is undeniable.

Among the reactions from Christians to Constantine’s conversion and the subsequent changes in the church, some embraced the new status and opportunities, while others expressed concern about the potential compromises and challenges that came with being aligned with imperial power. Five postures from early Christians regarding Constantine’s conversion are:

Grateful and uncritical: Constantine ended gladiatorial games, punished sexual crimes more harshly, improved the lives of women, slaves and children, returned confiscated property, built churches, oulawed inhumane treatment of animals, and supported the poor. Many Christians were simply grateful for these benefits and did not question his motives or the implications of his conversion.

Fleeing to remote places: Some Christians, particularly monks and ascetics, chose to withdraw from society and seek solitude in remote areas. They were concerned about the potential corruption and compromises that could arise from the church’s close association with imperial power.

Break away from the majority church: Some Christians, such as the 

Donatists in North Africa, rejected the authority of the mainstream church that was now aligned with the empire. They believed that the church had compromised its purity and integrity by accepting imperial support.

Pagan reactions: Some pagans viewed Constantine’s conversion as a betrayal of traditional Roman values and religious practices. They saw Christianity as a threat to the established order and resisted its growing influence. One example is Emperor Julian the Apostate (r. 361-363 A.D.), who attempted to revive paganism and reduce the influence of Christianity during his brief reign.

Critical but engaged: Some Christians, such as 

Arius and 

Athanasius, engaged in theological debates and controversies regarding the nature of Christ and the relationship between the Father and the Son. They were critical of certain aspects of the church’s alignment with imperial power but remained actively involved in shaping Christian doctrine and practice.

Regarding the leaders who were critical but engaged with Constantine’s conversion, Lesslie Newbigin will state that:

Much has been written about the harm done to the cause of the gospel when Constantine accepted baptism, and it is not difficult to expand on this theme. But could any other choice have been made? When the ancient classical world [...] ran out of spiritual fuel and turned to the church as the one society that could hold a disintegrating world together, should the church have refused the appeal and washed its hands of responsibility for the political order? [...]

It could not do so if it was to be faithful to its origins in Israel and the ministry of Jesus. It is easy to see with hindsight how quickly the church fell into the temptations of worldly power. It is easy to point [...] to the glaring contradictions between the Jesus of the Gospels and his followers occupying the seats of power and wealth. And yet we have to ask, would God’s purpose as it is revealed in Scripture have been better served, if the church had refused all political responsibility, if there had never been a “Christian” Europe, if all the churches for the past two thousand years had lived as persecuted minorities [...]? I find it hard to think so.

Jerome (c. 342-420 A.D.) was a priest, theologian, and historian, best known for his translation of the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate) and his extensive writings on Christian theology and asceticism. He is often depicted as a grumpy and fiery personality, known for his sharp wit and strong opinions.

The Vulgate became the standard Latin version of the Bible for the Western Church and had a profound influence on Christian theology and biblical scholarship for centuries. 

Augustine, though, criticized the effort due to some changes Jerome made compared to the Septuagint version commonly used at the time.

Pope Damasus I commissioned Jerome to produce this reliable and accurate Latin translation of the Bible.

Jerome also found a great deal of support from wealthy women, such as Paula and her daughter, Eustochium, who were dedicated to the ascetic life.

Due to his temper, Jerome made many enemies in Rome. After Damausus’s death in 384 AD, Jerome lost his protector and decided to leave the city. He moved to Bethlehem, where he established a monastery and continued his scholarly work. Paula and Eustochium followed him there. Paula founded a convent nearby.

Jerome passed a few months after Eustochium’s death in 420 AD. He would be buried next to her in the Church of the Nativity in Bethlehem.

In the Greek culture, the leaders are the philosophers. In the Roman culture, the leaders are the politicians and military leaders. In the early church, the leader is Jesus Christ.

As 4th century Christian leaders theologically articulated the nature of leadership, they were intentionally transforming Greco-Roman 

paideia, a powerfully influential tradition in ancient culture. 

Paideia is the process of forming ideal citizens in a wise way of life. This formation process had been developed over 1,000 years and involved training in rhetoric, philosophy, mentoring, moral modeling, etc.

By adapting Greco-Roman 

paideia into a Christian process of formation, Christian leaders transformed their culture as rapidly and profoundly as any period of Christian history.

This transformation was accelerated by Emperor Constantine’s conversion to Christianity and the subsequent adoption of Christianity as the favored religion of the Roman Empire. This shift in political power had significant implications for church leadership and organization. We will explore three ways in which the 

paideia of church leadership was transformed by church leaders at the time.

And:

records.content:
The goal of leadership is to form a thriving human being.

On the surface, this goal is similar to Greco-Roman 

paideia, but the definition of a thriving human being is quite different.

The leadership theology of the early church could be summarized as follows:

Glory of God ➜ thriving human being

Thriving human being ➜ person in communion with God. i.e., the end is in the beginning: union/communion with God is the original purpose for which we were created and the end goal of salvation.

A person in communion with God ➜ a person conformed to Jesus

A person conformed to Jesus ➜ a person who loves God and neighbor

Therefore, a leader’s role is psychagogy, that is, guiding souls to union with God (i.e., toward greater love).

In Greco-Roman 

paideia, philosophical schools were engaged in psychagogy, the guidance of souls into a wise way of life. So early Christian leaders argued that the school of the truest philosophy (the church) was also engaged in psychagogy, in a soul therapy which was guiding people into maturity in Christ which is the wisest way of life.

The Apostle Paul was a model of Christian psychagogy

Each phrase of his letters was calibrated precisely to the needs of the souls he was guiding. The early church read Paul as a pastor and preacher and consummate spiritual director, not a systematic theologian. Early church pastors sought to imitate Paul by guiding people toward faith, hope and love.

Early Christian bishops saw themselves first and foremost as guides of souls, not as administrative officials, not as resident systematic theologians, not as religiously-oriented psychologists. Above all, pastoral leaders were spiritual guides in the process of being conformed to the image of Christ.

Of course, being a spiritual guide got you involved in a lot of human affairs: deciding disputes, supporting the needy (e.g., challenging exploiters in times of famine), showing hospitality to strangers, standing up to abusive emperors and others whose moral example was witnessed by the public.

Psychagogy, the process of guiding souls to conform to Christ, is an extremely difficult task. We humans do not conform easily to becoming better lovers of God and others, because our loves are confused and disordered.

Gregory of Nazianzus says that “The leadership of men and women, the craftiest and most complicated of all creatures, seems to me the art of arts and the science of sciences.”

The primary means to guide people to greater union with God included:

Character modeling

Communal practices:  prayer, fasting, eucharist, charity, etc.

Teaching

Each of these means was used in Greco-Roman 

paideia, but Christians transformed their content and methods.

Ephesians 4

Ephesians 4 as an example of what a leader should do: equip the saints for the work of ministry, for building up the body of Christ.

The 4th and 5th centuries were a remarkable period of leadership in the early Christian church. This era saw the emergence of some of the most influential theologians, bishops, and church fathers who played pivotal roles in shaping Christian doctrine, defending the faith against heresies, and guiding the church through times of change and challenge.

The list of prominent leaders from this period (313-600 A.D.) includes:

Athanasius (the black dwarf)

Cappadocians:

Gregory of Nazianzus (the Theologian)

Basil of Caesarea (the Churchman)

Gregory of Nyssa (the Philosopher)

Macrina (the Teacher)

John Chrysostom (the Golden Mouth)

Jerome  (the Grump at Bethlehem)

Ambrose of Milan (statesman turned bishop)

Augustine (theologian of love)

We turn now to a brief overview of each of these leaders and their contributions to the church during this transformative period.

Professor Rylaarsdam mentioned the concept of Biblical worship as the Bible being brought alive to all five senses. Baptism is a great example of that, as it involves physical actions (immersion in water), auditory elements (words spoken during the baptism), and visual components (the symbolism of cleansing and new life).

The catechumenate process culminated in baptism, which was not only a rite of initiation but also a profound act of discipleship. Baptism symbolized the believer’s identification with the death, burial, and resurrection of Jesus Christ (Romans 6:3-4). It marked the beginning of a new life in Christ and a commitment to follow Him.

Baptism was typically performed by immersion in water, signifying the washing away of sin and the believer’s new life in Christ. The act of immersion itself was a powerful symbol of dying to the old self and being raised to new life (Colossians 2:12).

In this class we will explore the significance of baptism in the early church and its role in forming disciples. We will also discuss how baptism served as a public declaration of faith and a means of grace for the believer.

The most common place to perform baptisms in the early church were the house-churches. These were private homes where Christians gathered for worship, fellowship, and instruction. House-churches provided a more intimate and communal setting for baptism, allowing new believers to be welcomed into the Christian community.

That is to say that ideally baptism should be performed in a place where there is plenty of water, as many examples from the Bible, including Jesus’ baptism in the Jordan River (Matthew 3:13-17).

The house at Duras-Europos was built shortly after 200 A.D. and adapted to be used as a Christian meeting place. One room was enlarged to hold around 100 people, with a small platform for the bishop, and in the corner a baptismal font.

Baptismal Font

Baptismal fonts are usually located at the entrance of the church building, symbolizing the entry into the Christian life and reminding the congregation of their own baptism as they enter the worship space.

Justin Martyr on Baptism

“And on the day called Sunday an assembly is held in one place of all who live in town or country, and the records of the apostles or the writings of the prophets are read for as long as time allows. Then, when the reader has finished, the president in a discourse admonishes and exhorts [us] to imitate these good things. Then we all stand up together and send up prayers; and as we said before, when we have finished praying, bread and wine and water are brought up, and the president likewise sends up prayers and thanksgivings to the best of his ability, and the people assent, saying the Amen; and the [elements over which] thanks have been given are distributed, and everyone partakes; and they are sent through the deacons to those who are not present.  And the wealthy who so desire give what they wish, as each chooses; and what is collected is deposited with the president.  He helps orphans and widows, and those who through sickness or any other cause are in need, and those in prison, and strangers sojourning among us; in a word, he takes care of all those who are in need.  We hold this common gathering on Sunday, since it is the first day, on which God transforming darkness and matter made the universe, and Jesus Christ our Savior rose from the dead on the same day.”

Justin Martyr, 155 AD

Baptism in the early church was not merely a ritual but a profound proclamation of the gospel. It symbolized the believer’s union with Christ in His death and resurrection, signifying the forgiveness of sins and the gift of new life (Acts 2:38; Romans 6:4).

Some of the significant theological themes associated with baptism in the early church include:

Theme

Significance

Romans 6:3; Colossians 2:12; Mark 10:38

Belonging to the Church

The Holy Spirit

Acts 2:38; 1 Corinthians 6:11

Forgiveness of Sins

New Creation/Life

Becoming a new creation in Christ.

John 3:5; Titus 3:5

The experience of baptism is also connected to the concept of anemnesis, or remembrance, where the believer recalls and participates in the saving events of Christ’s life, death, and resurrection. Through baptism, believers are reminded of their identity in Christ and their call to live as His disciples in the world.

Anemnesis

Anemnesis is a Greek term meaning “remembrance” or “memorial.” In Christian liturgy, it refers to the act of recalling and proclaiming the significant events of salvation history, particularly the life, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ. Anemnesis serves to connect believers with the foundational events of their faith, fostering a sense of continuity and participation in the ongoing story of God’s redemptive work.

The process of Christian initiation in the early church typically involved several key steps:

Catechumenate: As discussed in the previous lecture, this was a period of instruction and preparation for new converts.

Pre-baptismal Rites: Before baptism, catechumens often underwent rites of exorcism to renounce Satan and his works. They were also anointed with oil as a sign of being set apart for God.

Baptism: The actual act of baptism, usually performed by immersion in water, symbolizing the washing away of sin and the new life in Christ.

Chrismation: After baptism, the new believer was anointed with holy oil (chrism), symbolizing the gift of the Holy Spirit.

Eucharist: The newly baptized would then participate in the Lord’s Supper, signifying their full inclusion in the Christian community.

Instruction and Discipleship: Following baptism, new believers would continue to receive instruction and be nurtured in their faith as they grew in discipleship. This step was also known as mystagogy.

Worship and Baptism

Not only is much Scripture heard, it is also seen and experienced through the rituals and symbols of baptism.

Theological use of biblical symbols: oil, numbers, shapes, clothes, milk and honey, kissing, temperature and movement of water, etc.

In biblical essentials, unity; in details diversity

Before the actual baptism, several important ceremonies and rituals were typically observed to prepare the catechumens for this significant step in their faith journey:

1 - Renunciation of Sin

The catechumens publicly renounced their former way of life, including any ties to paganism or sin, as a preparation for their new life in Christ. This part of the ceremony would also involve exorcisms to symbolically free the catechumens from the influence of evil spirits.
2 - Led to the Baptismal Font

The catechumens were ceremonially led to the baptismal font, often accompanied by prayers and hymns, symbolizing their journey towards new life.

Mark 15:22 mentions Jesus being led to Golgotha, which can be seen as a parallel to the catechumens being led to baptism.

Mark 15:46 states that Jesus was laid in a tomb after his crucifixion, symbolizing the death to sin that baptism represents.

3 - Removal of Clothing

Catechumens would remove their clothing before baptism, symbolizing the shedding of their old self and the beginning of a new life in Christ.

Gn 2:25 states that Adam and his wife were both naked and felt no shame, symbolizing the innocence and purity of the newly baptized.

Col 3:9-10 speaks of putting off the old self and putting on the new self, which aligns with the symbolism of removing clothing before baptism.

Ephesians 4:22-24 also emphasizes this transformation, urging believers to put off their old self and be renewed in the spirit of their minds.

John 19:23-25 describes the soldiers dividing Jesus’ garments and casting lots for his clothing, which can be seen as a foreshadowing of the believer’s new identity in Christ.

4 - Anointing with Oil

Catechumens were often anointed with oil before baptism, symbolizing their consecration to God and the presence of the Holy Spirit.

Luke 10:34 describes the Good Samaritan anointing the wounds of the injured man, symbolizing healing and restoration.

James 5:14 encourages the anointing of the sick with oil in the name of the Lord, symbolizing spiritual healing and empowerment.

Mark 6:13 mentions the apostles anointing the sick with oil and healing them, symbolizing the power of the Holy Spirit at work.

Hebrews 1:9 speaks of God’s anointing of the Son with the oil of gladness, symbolizing joy and divine favor.

Psalm 23:4-5 describes God anointing the psalmist’s head with oil, symbolizing blessing and abundance.

Psalm 45:7 speaks of God’s anointing of the king with the oil of gladness above his companions, symbolizing honor and divine approval.

Romans 11:24 mentions being grafted in by faith, which can be symbolized by the anointing with oil as a sign of inclusion in God’s people.

Anointing with Oil

For Cyril of Jerusalem, anointing is a symbol of the share that the candidate will have in the richness of Christ the true olive tree.

Other symbols related to anointing with oil:

protection against evil (e.g. Psalm 23:4-5)

preparation for combat with the devil: candidates are rubbed with oil like an athlete, Christ’s athlete

ownership, like the branding of a sheep

These pre-baptismal ceremonies emphasized the transformative nature of baptism and the commitment required to follow Christ.

The actual act of baptism, usually performed by immersion in water, symbolizing the washing away of sin and the new life in Christ. But not any water! The early church preferred “living water,” such as rivers, streams, or springs, which symbolized the life-giving and cleansing power of God. Also, luke warm water was avoided, as it could symbolize spiritual lukewarmness (Revelation 3:16).

Baptism according to the Didache

“Now about baptism: this is how to baptize. Give public instruction on all these points, and then immerse in running water, ‘in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.’ If you do not have running water, immerse in some other. If you cannot in cold, then in warm. If you have neither, then pour water on the head three times ‘in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.’ Before the baptism, the one who baptizes and the one being baptized must fast, and any others who can. And you must tell the one being baptized to fast one or two days beforehand” (Didache 7:1-4).

The reason for running water can be found in many Scripture passages that highlight the symbolism of water in relation to spiritual cleansing and new life:

Genesis 1:2 - “Now the earth was formless and empty, darkness was over the surface of the deep, and the Spirit of God was hovering over the waters.” This passage emphasizes the creative power of God associated with water.

Exodus 14:21-22 - “Then Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and all that night the Lord drove the sea back with a strong east wind and turned it into dry land. The waters were divided, and the Israelites went through the sea on dry ground, with a wall of water on their right and on their left.” This event symbolizes deliverance and new beginnings through water.

Matthew 3:16 - “As soon as Jesus was baptized, he went up out of the water. At that moment heaven was opened, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and alighting on him.” This passage highlights the significance of baptism in Jesus’ life and ministry.

Mark 1:10 - “Just as Jesus was coming up out of the water, he saw heaven being torn open and the Spirit descending on him like a dove.” This passage reinforces the connection between baptism and the presence of the Holy Spirit.

Luke 3:21-22 - “When all the people were being baptized, Jesus was baptized too. And as he was praying, heaven was opened and the Holy Spirit descended on him in bodily form like a dove. And a voice came from heaven: ‘You are my Son, whom I love; with you I am well pleased.’” This passage emphasizes the divine affirmation of Jesus’ identity through baptism.

John 5:3 - “In these lay a great number of disabled people—blind, lame, and paralyzed—waiting for the moving of the waters.” This passage highlights the healing power associated with water.

John 7:38 - “Whoever believes in me, as Scripture has said, rivers of living water will flow from within them.” This passage emphasizes the life-giving nature of water in relation to faith in Christ.

Revelation 22:1 - “Then the angel showed me the river of the water of life, as clear as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb.” This passage symbolizes eternal life and divine provision through water.

Early Christian architecture often incorporated specific elements related to baptism, reflecting its significance in the life of the church. Some of these elements include:

After baptism, several practices are often observed to help the newly baptized integrate into the Christian community and grow in their faith. These practices may include:

First Communion: The newly baptized may receive their first communion, participating fully in the Eucharist and the life of the church.
