First Communion

The newly baptized receives their first communion

Participation in the Eucharist and life of the church

John 6:53-58; 1 Cor. 11:23-26

Cyril of Jerusalem annointed the newly baptized with chrism on various parts of the body, symbolizing their participation in the life of Christ:

On the forehead: to lose the shame of Adam (Exodus 28:36-38; Ezekiel 9:4; Revelation 13:16-17)

On the ears: to hear the word of God (Isaiah 35:5; Isaiah 50:5; Matthew 11:15; Mark 7:33)

On the nose: to smell the fragrance of Christ (2 Corinthians 2:14-16; Ephesians 5:2)

On the chest: to be armed against the devil (Isaiah 59:17; Ephesians 6:14; 1Timothy 5:8)

The newly baptized are then welcomed into the Christian community, exchanging the “kiss of peace” with other believers (Romans 16:16; 1 Corinthians 16:20; 2 Corinthians 13:12; 1 Thessalonians 5:26; 1 Peter 5:14).

They are then invited to participate in the Eucharist, symbolizing their full inclusion in the body of Christ (1 Corinthians 10:16-17; 11:23-26). In their first communion, they receive a compound of honey and milk together with the wine and bread, symbolizing the sweetness and nourishment of the Christian life, as well as the entrance in the promised land (Psalm 19:10; Proverbs 24:13-14; Isaiah 7:15; 1 Peter 2:2).

As they leave the service, they are incited to give alms to the poor, symbolizing their new commitment to love and serve others as followers of Christ (Matthew 25:35-40; Luke 3:11; Acts 20:35; James 1:27).

Baptism Today

A discussion was held about how we understand all the symbols and rituals of baptism today. Some questions to consider:
If a congregation baptizes

by sprinkling a few drops of water

that is often lukewarm

and stagnant

in a font that looks like a bird bath

(often shoved out of sight on most Sundays)

and no one fasts beforehand...

Does any of this matter?

hierarchy.lvl2: Separation Between Baptism and Holy Supper
Separation Between Baptism and Holy Supper

records.content:
In the Early Church, baptism and the Lord’s Supper were united. Baptism and the post-baptismal anointing (later referred to as confirmation) led directly to the Table. E.g., Cyprian and Augustine practiced infant baptism AND infant communion.

The Eastern Church has always maintained the unity of baptism and the Eucharist. In the Western Church, however, a separation developed over time. By the Middle Ages, it became common for baptized infants to wait until they were older (often around age seven) to receive their first communion.

The practice of infant communion continued in the West until the 13th century, but several medieval developments gradually ended the practice.

Some of the reasons for the change in the Western Church include:

Strengthening the power of bishops: In the West, only a bishop was allowed to confirm a baptism. Since a bishop was not available in some areas for many years, infant participation in Communion was sometimes delayed.

Medieval mentality

Power to the hierarchy!

Some bishops would pass by some villages for years without visiting baptizing from the horseback as passing by.

The doctrine of transubstantiation (13th cent.): The substance of bread and wine changes into the actual body and blood of Jesus.

Medieval mentality

Don’t let children drop Jesus’ actual body on the floor or slobber into his real blood!

Heavy penitential piety: Kids can’t do serious penance like adults can.

Medieval mentality

Kids shouldn’t come to the Eucharist until their penance makes them worthy.

Making up a doctrine: confirmation. In this so-called sacrament, individuals confirm their place in the church.

Medieval mentality

Confirmation is a sacrament even though its biblical support is underwhelming.

Parents who thought confirmation wasn’t a sacrament were punished: Parents and their kids were banned from communion if the kids were not confirmed.

Medieval mentality

Confirmation is a sacrament and people who disobey the hierarchy must be punished.

In the 16th century, Reformers clarified that confirmation is not a sacrament, and renamed it “public profession of faith.”

1 Corinthians 11 is the proof text, but John Calvin’s new interpretation downplays the literary and historical context and misinterprets “body” in 11:27.

“We offer poison [...] to our tender children” at the Supper, for it is vain to expect them “to distinguish rightly the holiness of Christ’s body.”

The Reformed tradition inherited a MEDIEVAL, not a Reformed, practice.

The catechumenate was an essential part of the early Christian community, serving as a period of instruction and preparation for new converts before their baptism. This process was not only about imparting knowledge but also about fostering spiritual growth and integration into the Christian way of life.

The catechumenate typically lasted for several months, during which catechumens (those preparing for baptism) would receive teachings on Christian doctrine, ethics, and practices. They would also participate in communal worship and engage in acts of charity and service.

To understand the catechumenate, it is important to consider its historical context. In the early centuries of Christianity, conversion to the faith was a significant decision that often involved a complete transformation of one’s life. The catechumenate provided a structured framework for this transformation, ensuring that new believers were adequately prepared for the responsibilities and challenges of Christian discipleship.

The Roman Empire had a mentality that every citizen should be shaped through the process of education and initiation into civic life. Paideia was the Greek term for this process of education and formation. The catechumenate can be seen as a Christian adaptation of this broader cultural practice, where new converts were initiated into the Christian community and its values. A “Christian paideia” was being formed through the catechumenate.

Etymology of Catechumenate

The term “catechumenate” comes from the Greek word “katecheo,” which means “to instruct” or “to teach orally,” especially in the rudiments of a subject and a skill. The term also refers to the act of reporting an important event.

hierarchy.lvl2: The Missionary Aspect of the Catechumenate
The Missionary Aspect of the Catechumenate

records.content:
The catechumenate was not only a process of individual transformation but also a communal and missionary endeavor. The early church saw the catechumenate as a way to nurture new believers and equip them for active participation in the life and mission of the Christian community.

The main goals were to transform the new belivers and detox them from their previous pagan formation. For that, the catechumenate focused on several key aspects:

Provide a non polytheistic worldview: The catechumenate helped new converts understand the Christian worldview, which was monotheistic and centered on the worship of the one true God. This was a significant departure from the polytheistic beliefs of the surrounding culture.

Provide a non syncretistic religious practice: The catechumenate emphasized the distinctiveness of Christian worship and practices, helping catechumens to develop a clear understanding of Christian rituals and sacraments.

Foster ethical transformation: The catechumenate included teachings on Christian ethics and moral conduct, encouraging catechumens to live in accordance with the teachings of Jesus and the apostles.

Enable people to remain faithful in the face of persecution: The catechumenate prepared new believers to face potential persecution and challenges to their faith, equipping them with the spiritual resources and community support needed to remain steadfast.

To detoxify new believers from their previous pagan formation, the catechumenate employed various methods, including teaching the Scriptures as a way to renarrate their lives through the Biblical stories. Also, the process of formation involved:

witness by one’s way of life

baptism

prayer, preaching, eucharist, and other practices of the Christian community

witness by one’s way of life (yes, again!)

The identity formation would instill the idea that you belong to Jesus’ community, and that you are to live as a disciple of Jesus in the world. This new identity would then shape how catechumens interacted with the surrounding culture and engaged in mission. Therefore, the catechumenate can be seen as a bridge to help pagans cross over from their previous worldview and practices to a new life in Christ. At the same time, they are making their lives more attractive to the surrounding culture, as a testimony of the transforming power of the gospel.

hierarchy.lvl2: Witnessing by One’s Way of Life
Witnessing by One’s Way of Life

records.content:
One of the most powerful aspects of the catechumenate was the emphasis on witnessing by one’s way of life. Catechumens were encouraged to live out their faith in practical ways, demonstrating the transformative power of the gospel through their actions and interactions with others. This included acts of charity, hospitality, and service to those in need. By embodying the teachings of Jesus, catechumens served as living testimonies to the truth and relevance of the Christian faith.

We can attribute the growth of the early church in part to the witness of catechumens and new believers who lived out their faith in compelling ways. Their lives served as a powerful testimony to the surrounding culture, attracting others to the Christian community and inspiring them to explore the faith for themselves.

It is quite paramount to emphasize that the early church did not grow because:

people were compelled to join through coercion or social pressure

becoming a Christian was attractive because of material benefits or social status

there was an organized evangelistic program to win converts

worship services were entertaining or emotionally stimulating

The attraction were the Christians themselves, through their way of life. The early Christians demonstrated a radical commitment to love, service, and community that stood in stark contrast to the prevailing values of the Roman Empire. Their lives were marked by integrity, compassion, and a deep sense of purpose, which drew others to the faith.

Early Christians were focused on developing practices and habits of character that would contrast with the surrounding culture.

The Goal of Early Christian Formation from the Canons of Hippolytus

The goal is that the church “may shine with virtue, not before each other but also before the Gentiles so they may imitate them and become Christians.”

Some of the practices that early Christians developed included:

energetically feeding poor people,

providing free burial,

caring for boys and girls who lacked property and parents,

being attentive to aged slaves, prisoners, miners, travelers,

rescuing exposed infants (often girls) from garbage heaps and raising them as their own children,

caring for desperately ill pagans during the plague,

creating a ‘sociological impossibility’ by breaking barriers between rich/poor, male/female, slave/free, Greek/barbarian,

radiating hope and joy in a culture of despair, anxiety, uncertainty,

practicing chastity / marital faithfulness in sex-saturated culture,

simplicity and generosity amidst consumption and accumulation,

forgiving their executioners.

The catechumenate typically involved several stages, including:

Inquiry: Individuals interested in becoming Christians would express their desire to join the faith community. They would meet with church leaders and receive initial instruction on the basics of Christian belief and practice.

Catechesis: This was the main period of instruction and formation, where catechumens would receive more in-depth teachings on Christian doctrine, ethics, and practices. They would also participate in communal worship and engage in acts of charity and service.

Preparation for Baptism: As catechumens neared the end of their formation, they would undergo additional preparation for baptism, including spiritual disciplines such as fasting, prayer, and confession.

Baptism: The catechumenate would culminate in the baptism of the new believers, typically during the Easter Vigil. This sacrament marked their formal entry into the Christian community and their new life in Christ.

Post-Baptismal Catechesis: After baptism, new believers would continue to receive instruction and support as they integrated into the Christian community and lived out their faith.

Each catechumen would be assigned a sponsor or mentor from the Christian community to guide them through the process and provide support and encouragement.

The cathecumenate process intended to:

Renarrate the lives of new believers through the Biblical story

Instill a new identity as a disciple of Jesus

Detoxify from previous pagan formation

Reshape habits and practices to align with Christian virtues and make their lives attractive to the surrounding culture

The instructions content would include:

Biblical stories

Creeds

Lord’s Prayer

Ethical teachings: the Sermon on the Mount and the 10 Commandments

Some report from Egeria about the catechumenate in Jerusalem (c. 380 AD)

“There has been teaching on all the Scriptures from six to nine in the morning all through Lent, three hours’ catechesis a day.  At ordinary services when the bishop sits and preaches, ladies and sisters, the faithful utter exclamations, but when they come and hear him explaining the catechesis, their exclamations are far louder, God is my witness; and when it is related and interpreted like this they ask questions on each point.”

Some of the teachings of the catechumenate that shaped early Christian ethics included:

Christians are meant to take any job that allows them to live out their faith authentically, even if it means facing persecution or hardship. Some jobs though are incompatible with Christian discipleship, such as being a soldier or participating in idolatrous practices.

Carpentry, painting, engraving, stucco work? Christians must not contribute to manufacture of idols

Teacher or professor? Christians must beware of formative power of idolatrous pagan philosophy

Trade and business? Christians must not covet or be greedy

Civil appointment or military? Christians must not worship the Emperor or murder

The principles established during the catechumenate can still inform our understanding of Christian ethics and vocation today. As we navigate our own cultural context, we can ask learn from the early church’s emphasis on:

Missional mentality: living as witnesses to Christ in our daily lives

Communal instruction: engaging in ongoing learning and formation within the Christian community

Spiritual disciplines/practices: incorporating prayer, fasting, and study into daily life

Clear commitments: to Jesus, to Jesus’ community, to the Jesus’ way of life.

Mentoring:  a sponsor is both a teacher and a student.

Accountability: fostering a culture of mutual support and encouragement

Discipling “older” and “newer” Christians simultaneously

Rigorous discipline:  disciple means spiritual athlete; no spectators

Life-encompassing: integrating faith into all aspects of life

By embracing these principles, we can continue the legacy of the catechumenate and live out our faith in meaningful and transformative ways.

The canon of Scripture refers to the collection of books that are recognized as authoritative and inspired by God within the Christian tradition. The process of canonization was gradual and involved discernment by early church leaders and councils. The canon served as a safeguard against heretical teachings and provided a foundation for Christian doctrine.

The practical needs for a canon arose from several factors:

need for a set text for worship and teaching

need for devotional reading material

need for a source of theological reflection

need for a set text to translate into other languages

At 100 A.D., there was no fixed canon of Christian Scripture. The “New Testament” books were not yet collected and defined as “Scripture”. Still, early Christian writers (e.g., Polycarp and Ignatius) quote from the Gospels and Paul’s letters, as well as from other Christian writings and oral sources. Paul’s letters were collected late in the first century. Matthew, Mark and Luke were brought together by AD 150.

That is to say that by the mid-2nd century, there was a core collection of Christian writings that were widely recognized and used in the church. However, there were still debates about which books should be included in the canon.

The Muratorian Canon is the earliest known list of New Testament books, dating to around 200 A.D. It includes most of the books that are now part of the New Testament, but it also excludes some books that are now considered canonical (e.g., Hebrews, 1 and 2 Peter, 3 John) and includes some books that are now considered apocryphal (e.g., The Shepherd of Hermas, The Revelation of Peter).

By 250 A.D., there was a more widely accepted canon of Christian Scripture, which included the four Gospels, the Acts of the Apostles, the Pauline Epistles, and some other writings. However, there were still debates about certain books, such as Hebrews, James, 2 Peter, Jude, The Shepherd of Hermas, and Letter to Barnabas.

By 300 A.D., there were still a dispute over books like James, 2 Peter, 2 and 3 John and Jude. Some books were excluded such as The Shepherd of Hermas and The Revelation of Peter.

That is to say that by the early 4th century, there was a more or less settled canon of Christian Scripture, but there were still some debates and variations in different regions.

hierarchy.lvl2: The Council of Carthage in 397 A.D.
The Council of Carthage in 397 A.D.

records.content:
The Council of Carthage in 397 A.D. is often cited as a significant moment in the formal recognition of the New Testament canon. The council produced a list of canonical books that closely resembles the modern New Testament. This list included the 27 books that are now universally recognized as canonical.

The apparent criteria for canonicity included:

Apostolic authorship or connection

Orthodox content consistent with Christian teaching

Antiquity of the text

Usage in liturgical practice by the church

The books listed in the Council of Carthage’s canon are:

The four Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John)

The Acts of the Apostles

The Pauline Epistles (Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, 1 and 2 Thessalonians, 1 and 2 Timothy, Titus, Philemon)

The General Epistles (Hebrews, James, 1 and 2 Peter, 1, 2, and 3 John, Jude)

The Book of Revelation

The definition of the 

canon at the Council of Carthage helped to solidify the New Testament as we know it today. However, it is important to note that the canon was not universally accepted immediately, and some regional variations persisted for some time. The process of canonization was gradual and involved discernment by church leaders and councils over several centuries.

Another question that would come up later is the question of how to interpret the canon. And that’s the direction will turn next, as we look at the life and works of Origen of Alexandria.

hierarchy.lvl1: The Creeds (or a Rule of Faith)
The Creeds (or a Rule of Faith)

records.content:
The creeds are concise statements of Christian belief that summarize the essential doctrines of the faith. They serve as a “rule of faith” that helps to define orthodox Christian beliefs and distinguish them from heretical teachings, such as those found in Gnosticism.

The main purposes of the creeds are to:

organize teaching for catechumens

express identity at baptism

unify the church in all times and places

express communal faith in worship

guide reading of Scripture

fight heresy

The most well-known creeds in Christian history are the Apostles’ Creed and the Nicene Creed. The Apostles’ Creed is an early statement of Christian belief that likely developed from the baptismal confession used in the early church. It summarizes key beliefs about God the Father, Jesus Christ, and the Holy Spirit.

hierarchy.lvl1: The Creeds (or a Rule of Faith)
The Creeds (or a Rule of Faith)

records.content:
The Apostles’ Creed is one of the oldest and most widely used creeds in Christianity. It is traditionally attributed to the apostles, although it was likely developed over time by early Christian communities. The creed affirms essential Christian doctrines, including the nature of God, the incarnation, crucifixion, resurrection, and ascension of Jesus Christ, as well as beliefs about the Holy Spirit, the church, and eternal life.



The Apostles Creed (ca. 1550–1600). Each of the fifteen compartments in this tapestry contains a single scene representing an article of the Apostles’ Creed, a set of declarations of Christian belief dating back to the fourth century. One of few surviving tapestries to depict this subject, this piece is unique for its inclusion of every article in a single hanging, without any accompanying inscriptions. The straightforward, even provincial design of the compositions makes them easily legible, unfolding like a comic strip from top to bottom. The series opens with God creating heaven and earth and ends with an image of everlasting life. Within the context of the church, such tapestries offered visual lessons that would have been used in religious instruction. 

Source

I believe in God, the Father almighty, Creator of heaven and earth, and in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord, who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died and was buried; he descended into hell; on the third day he rose again from the dead; he ascended into heaven, and is seated at the right hand of God the Father almighty; from there he will come to judge the living and the dead.

I believe in the Holy Spirit, the holy catholic Church, the communion of saints, the forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the body, and life everlasting.

Amen.

The Nicene Creed was formulated at the First Council of Nicaea in 325 AD and later expanded at the First Council of Constantinople in 381 AD. It was created to address various heresies, particularly Arianism, which denied the full divinity of Jesus Christ. The Nicene Creed affirms the belief in the Trinity and the full divinity and humanity of Jesus Christ.



Icon depicting Constantine the Great, accompanied by the bishops of the First Council of Nicaea (325), holding the Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed of 381. First line of main text in Greek: Πιστεύω εἰς ἕνα Θ[εό]ν, πατέρα παντοκράτορα, ποιητὴν οὐρανοῦ κ[αὶ] γῆς,. Translation: “We believe in one God, the Father, the Almighty, Maker of heaven and earth.”

records.content:
Jesus is the most amazing, confounding, alarming, and captivating person ever to walk the planet. Even as the early church loved and worshiped Jesus, they found describing him beyond available words. Over time they assembled carefully formed truths about Jesus into creeds.  Creeds were one way to clearly describe and confess their faith in this most amazing person ever to live, and a way to invite novices into deeper understanding about who he is. We invite you to say a creed now as a way to enter into the mystery of Jesus.



In the early church, spiritual novices memorized and spoke creeds as a way to take in the faith and to let it grow deep inside.  At their baptism, new believers would say the creeds as their first statement of faith.  Veteran Christians would say it together to reinforce their own belief.  In that spirit, whether you’re a spiritual novice or a veteran, we invite you to say these ancient and time-tested words.



The church is not a place where we make up what we believe.  It is a place where we receive the true story of the world.  In the New Testament, the Apostle Paul talks about this faithful handing down of the gospel.  Let’s use the words of the Apostles’ Creed to receive the story that has been handed down.

“We are not brains on a stick that will enable our entry to the Pleroma.”

Christians should avoid a salvation-by-knowledge mentality. That is, avoid the mentality that salvation is about acquiring the right knowledge or correct beliefs in order to be saved.

Avoid the mentality that we can read the Bible without the guidance of tradition. Sola scriptura is misleading, a recipe for heresy. The Bible is our only infallible authority, but it is not our only authority. Without the guidance of tradition to read Scripture, we could be Gnostic Christians, Jehovah Witnesses, Mormons, etc.
Avoid “Star Trek Jesus,” a savior who beams our souls up out of this world. “Star Trek Jesus” has nothing to do with daily human existence.

Avoid a worldview that confines God to a spiritual realm that is disconnected from the rest of creation. This is a spiritualizing tendency—the cultural inclination to imagine that one can talk meaningfully about theology apart from any substantive reflection on politics, economics, or culture; acting as if theology is somehow independent of or sealed off from these more mundane realities.

In his famous “Letter from a Birmingham Jail,” Martin Luther King Jr. critiques the white moderate for being more devoted to “order” than to justice, for preferring a negative peace which is the absence of tension to a positive peace which is the presence of justice. This attitude reflects a dualistic separation between the sacred and the secular, where social issues are dismissed as irrelevant to the gospel. King writes:

“I must confess that over the past few years I have been gravely disappointed with the white moderate. I have almost reached the regrettable conclusion that the Negro’s great stumbling block in his stride toward freedom is not the White Citizen’s Counciler or the Ku Klux Klanner, but the white moderate … In the midst of blatant injustices inflicted upon the Negro, I have watched white churchmen stand on the sideline and mouth pious irrelevancies and sanctimonious trivialities. In the midst of a mighty struggle to rid our nation of racial and economic injustice, I have heard many ministers say: ‘Those are social issues, with which the gospel has no real concern.’ And I have watched many churches commit themselves to a completely other worldly religion which makes a strange, un-Biblical distinction between body and soul, between the sacred and the secular.”

Docetism was a prominent Gnostic belief that emerged in the early centuries of Christianity, asserting that Jesus Christ only appeared to have a physical body and did not truly possess one. The term “docetism” is derived from the Greek word “dokein,” which means “to seem” or “to appear.”

According to docetic teachings, Jesus was a purely spiritual being who merely took on the appearance of a human form, but his physical body was an illusion. This belief was rooted in the Gnostic worldview, which viewed the material world as inherently evil or corrupt, and therefore, it was inconceivable for a divine being to take on a physical body.

Docetism posed a significant challenge to orthodox Christian beliefs, particularly regarding the incarnation and the nature of Jesus Christ. The early church firmly rejected docetic teachings, emphasizing the full humanity and divinity of Jesus Christ as essential to the Christian faith. The 

Council of Nicaea in 325 CE and subsequent councils affirmed the orthodox understanding of Christ’s incarnation, rejecting docetism and other heresies that denied the true humanity of Jesus.

It is important to note that docetism is best understood as a collection of widespread tendencies rather than a movement originating from one person.



The Gospel of Peter, a Gnostic text discovered in the Nag Hammadi library, contains docetic elements that reflect the belief that Jesus’ physical form was an illusion. 

Source

“Error never shows itself in its naked reality, in order not to be discovered. On the contrary, it dresses elegantly, so that the unwary may be led to believe that it is more truthful than truth itself.” (Irenaeus of Lyons)

At this part of the course, we are concerned about what is the Gospel in the context of the early church. We have already seen how the early Christians understood their mission in the Hellenistic culture through the writings of the Apostolic Fathers. Now, we will explore the challenges that the early church faced in defining and defending the Gospel message, particularly in the context of Gnosticism.

In a context of polytheism, dualism, syncretism, and mystery religions, the early Christians had to articulate what they believed about Jesus Christ and his significance for salvation. Gnosticism, with its emphasis on secret knowledge (gnosis) and its dualistic worldview, posed a significant challenge to the early church’s understanding of the Gospel. Therefore, the church needs a story, a narrative that makes sense of who Jesus is, what he has done, and what it means for humanity. That is made through the creation of the creeds.

Sola Scriptura is a theological doctrine that asserts that the Bible is the sole infallible source of authority for Christian faith and practice. This doctrine emerged during the 20th century, known as the “Scripture Alone” principle, and is based on the works from the Protestant Reformation in the 16th century as a response to certain practices and teachings of the Roman Catholic Church, which reformers believed were not grounded in Scripture.

It is very relevant to reflect on the fact that Scripture Alone can be very misleading and even harmful if not properly understood. The early church did not have a New Testament canon as we have today. The canon was formed over several centuries, and the early Christians relied on oral tradition, apostolic teachings, and various writings that were considered authoritative at the time. Therefore, the early church had to rely on creeds, councils, and the guidance of the Holy Spirit to discern the true teachings of Christianity.

If we are to take Sola Scriptura seriously, we need to understand that the Bible itself points us to the community of faith, the church, as the context in which Scripture is interpreted and understood. The early church’s creeds and councils were not attempts to add to Scripture but rather to clarify and articulate the essential truths of the Christian faith in response to various challenges and heresies.

Therefore, we must rely on more than Scripture alone. We must also rely on:

Creed (the story, the narrative that makes sense of Scripture)

Canon (the authoritative books that make up Scripture)

Holy Spirit (the guide and teacher of the church)

Leaders (the teachers and pastors who help interpret and apply Scripture)

If any one of these is missing or misunderstood, our understanding of the Gospel can be distorted. That could be seen in the medieval church, where the leaders abused their authority, leading to corruption and the need for the Reformation. It could also be seen in some modern churches that reject creeds and traditions, leading to a fragmented and individualistic approach to faith.

Gnosticism was a diverse and complex religious movement that emerged in the early centuries of Christianity. It was characterized by its emphasis on secret knowledge (gnosis) as the key to salvation and its dualistic worldview, which posited a stark contrast between the spiritual and material realms.



A traveller peers through an opening in the firmament in this illustration from Camille Flammarion’s L’atmosphère : météorologie populaire (Paris: Hachette, 1888), p. 163

Gnostics believed that the material world was created by a lesser deity, often referred to as the Demiurge, who was distinct from the true, transcendent God. They viewed the material world as inherently evil or corrupt, while the spiritual realm was seen as pure and good. According to Gnostic beliefs, human beings contained a divine spark or spirit that was trapped within their physical bodies, and salvation involved awakening this divine spark through gnosis.

Gnosticism presented a significant challenge to the early Christian church, as it offered an alternative understanding of Jesus Christ and his mission. Gnostics often portrayed Jesus as a divine being who imparted secret knowledge to a select few, rather than as the incarnate Son of God who came to redeem humanity through his death and resurrection. This led to various Gnostic sects and teachings that diverged from orthodox Christian beliefs, prompting the early church to respond with creeds and councils to clarify the true nature of Christ and the Gospel message.

Therefore, we can define Gnosticism by the following characteristics:

Characteristic

Description

metaphysical dualism

Belief in two opposing realms: the spiritual (good) and the material (evil)

material world is wrong/meaningless/evil

The physical world is created by a lesser deity (Demiurge) and is inherently flawed

escape/“salvation” through esoteric knowledge

Salvation is achieved by acquiring secret knowledge (gnosis) that awakens the divine spark within

knowledge is given only to “insiders”

Gnosis is accessible only to a select group of individuals who are initiated into the Gnostic teachings

sense of powerlessness, therefore elaborate myths

Gnostic myths often involve complex cosmologies and narratives that explain the origin of the world and humanity’s plight

syncretistic

Gnosticism often incorporated elements from various religious traditions, including Christianity, Judaism, and paganism

ascetics or libertines

Gnostic groups varied in their ethical teachings, with some advocating for strict asceticism while others embraced libertine practices

From now onwards we will study the many different types of Gnosticism that emerged in the early centuries of Christianity, including Marcionism and Docetism, and how the early church responded to these challenges in order to defend and articulate the true Gospel message.

Some of the major Gnostic movements that existed in the early centuries of Christianity include:

Movement

Founder

Years of Existence

Description

c. 85–160 CE

Emphasized a radical dualism between the God of the Old Testament and the God of the New Testament; rejected the Old Testament and created a unique canon of Christian texts.

c. 100–160 CE

Developed a complex cosmology involving divine emanations (Aeons) and the concept of the Pleroma; emphasized the role of gnosis for salvation.

Asserted that Jesus Christ only appeared to have a physical body and did not truly possess one; denied the full humanity of Jesus.

Centered around the figure of Seth, the third son of Adam and Eve; developed elaborate myths about the creation of the world and the role of divine beings.

Founded by the prophet Mani; combined elements of Gnosticism, Christianity, Zoroastrianism, and Buddhism; emphasized a cosmic struggle between light and darkness.

These movements, among others, contributed to the rich and diverse landscape of Gnostic thought in the early Christian era. Each movement had its own unique beliefs, practices, and interpretations of Christian teachings, which often diverged significantly from orthodox Christianity. The early church responded to these challenges by developing 

creeds and doctrines that affirmed the true nature of Christ and the Gospel message, ultimately shaping the course of Christian theology and practice.

Marcionism was a significant Gnostic Christian movement founded by Marcion of Sinope (c. 85–160 CE). Marcion was a wealthy shipowner who became a prominent figure in the early Christian church. He is best known for his radical theological views, which led to his excommunication from the orthodox Christian community. He was the son of a bishop in Sinope, a city on the southern coast of the Black Sea (modern-day Turkey).

Marcion’s teachings were characterized by a strong dualism, which posited a distinction between the God of the Old Testament and the God of the New Testament. He believed that the God of the Old Testament was a lesser, vengeful deity (the 

Demiurge) who created the material world, while the true God revealed in Jesus Christ was a higher, benevolent being who offered salvation through grace. This radical reinterpretation of Scripture led Marcion to reject the Old Testament entirely and to create his own canon of Christian texts, which included an edited version of the Gospel of Luke and ten of Paul’s epistles.

Marcionism posed a significant challenge to the early church, as it forced Christian leaders to clarify their understanding of the relationship between the Old and New Testaments and to defend the unity of God’s revelation in Scripture. The movement ultimately led to the development of the orthodox Christian canon and the affirmation of the Old Testament as an integral part of the Christian faith.



Apostle John and Marcion of Sinope, from JPM Library MS 748, 11th century. 

Source

Marcion’s Community

After being accused of heresy and excommunicated from the orthodox Christian church around 144 CE, Marcion went on to establish his own church, which spread throughout the Roman Empire. Marcionism gained a significant following, particularly among Gentile Christians who were attracted to Marcion’s emphasis on grace and his rejection of Jewish law.

Valentinianism was one of the major Gnostic Christian movements in the second century, founded by Valentinus (c. 100–160 CE), a prominent Gnostic teacher. Valentinus taught a complex cosmology that involved a series of divine emanations (Aeons) from a supreme, unknowable God. According to Valentinian belief, the material world was created by a lesser deity, often identified with the God of the Old Testament, who was ignorant of the higher spiritual realities.

Valentinians believed that human beings contained a divine spark or seed that originated from the higher spiritual realm. This divine spark was trapped within the material body, and salvation involved awakening this spark through gnosis (knowledge) of one’s true spiritual nature and origin. Valentinian teachings emphasized the role of Jesus Christ as a revealer of this secret knowledge, who came to impart gnosis to those capable of receiving it.

Valentinianism also had a distinctive view of the church and sacraments. Valentinians often practiced a form of initiation that involved baptism and a special rite known as the “bridal chamber,” which symbolized the union of the soul with its divine origin.



Valentinian inscription from the grave stele of Flavia Sophe, referencing the bridal chamber. 

Source

Central to 

Valentinian cosmology is the concept of the Pleroma, the fullness of the divine realm inhabited by the Aeons. The Pleroma is a complex hierarchy of divine beings, each representing different aspects of the divine nature. At the top of this hierarchy is the ultimate God, from whom all Aeons emanate in pairs, reflecting a balance of masculine and feminine principles.

The fall of Sophia, one of the Aeons, led to the creation of the material world and the Demiurge, who is responsible for the flawed physical universe. The divine spark within humans is seen as a fragment of the Pleroma that has become trapped in the material world, and salvation involves returning this spark to its original divine source through gnosis.



This image is an illustration of the Gnostic figure Sophia, and it is a plate from the book Geheime Figuren der Rosenkreuzer (Secret Figures of the Rosicrucians) published in Altona, Germany, in 1785. 

Source: Wikimedia

The life outside the 

Pleroma is characterized by ignorance and suffering, as individuals are unaware of their true spiritual nature and are trapped in the material world. Three substances are identified in Valentinian thought:

Substance

Description

Hylic (matter)

The material world and physical body, associated with ignorance and corruption

Psychic (soul)

The soul or psyche, capable of receiving gnosis and salvation

Pneumatic (spirit)

The divine spark within humans, originating from the Pleroma

Irenaeus of Lyons, in his work Against Heresies, provides a distorted and ironic account of Valentinian cosmology:

“There exists a power which I call a Gourd. And along with this Gourd there exists a power which I call Utter-Emptiness. This Gourd and Emptiness, since they are one, produced a fruit, everywhere visible, eatable, and delicious, which fruit-language calls a Cucumber. Along with this Cucumber exists a power of the same essence, which I call a Melon. These powers—the Gourd, Utter-Emptiness, the Cucumber, and the Melon—brought forth the remaining multitude of the delirious melons of Valentinus.” (Against Heresies 1.11.4)

As the church growed and spread throughout the Roman Empire, they faced many challenges. Some of them were acknowledged such as persecution and misunderstandings from the surrounding culture. Other challenges came from within the Christian community itself, as different interpretations of Jesus’ life and teachings emerged. But one of the most significant challenges came from a group known as the Gnostics.

Let’s remember that the context where the early church lived was one of polytheism, dualism, syncretism, neo-platonism, and mystery religions. In this context, the early Christians had to articulate what they believed about Jesus Christ and his significance for salvation. Gnosticism, with its emphasis on secret knowledge (gnosis) and its dualistic worldview, posed a significant challenge to the early church’s understanding of the Gospel.

In order to defend and articulate the true Gospel message, the early church distinguished itself from Gnostic beliefs and the culture of their time by relying on these four pillars:

Creed (the story, the narrative that makes sense of Scripture)

Canon (the authoritative books that make up Scripture)

Holy Spirit (the guide and teacher of the church)

Leaders (the teachers and pastors who help interpret and apply Scripture)

This part of the course starts with an introduction to Gnosticism, followed by an exploration of two major Gnostic movements: Marcionism and Docetism. Finally, we will examine how the early church responded to these challenges through the development of the canon, creeds, and apostolic succession.

Irenaeus of Lyons (c. 130–202 AD) was an early Christian theologian and bishop known for his role in combating heresies, particularly Gnosticism. Born in Asia Minor, he later became the bishop of Lyons in Gaul (modern-day France). Irenaeus is best known for his work “Against Heresies” (Adversus Haereses), in which he systematically refuted Gnostic teachings and defended orthodox Christian doctrine.

Irenaeus was likely born in Smyrna (modern-day Izmir, Turkey) and was a student of Polycarp, who was himself a disciple of the Apostle John. This connection to the apostolic tradition gave Irenaeus a strong foundation in early Christian teachings. He later moved to Gaul, where he became the bishop of Lyons around 177 AD.

Irenaeus is possibly one of the biggest contributors to the development of Christian theology in the 2nd century. He is also known as the Theologian of Unities because of his emphasis on the unity of God, Christ, and the Church. These unities include:

Unity of God, as creator and redeemer

Unity of the person of Jesus, as Word and flesh

Unity of human history, as the working-out of a single, purposeful divine plan

Unity of revelation, both the OT Scriptures and the documents of the new covenant

Unity of the Christian faith throughout the world

Unity and continuity of the Church

Unity of the human being (body and soul), also in the resurrection

His stand on these unities was a direct response to Gnostic dualism, which posited a sharp divide between the material and spiritual worlds.

Irenaeus is also a pioneeer on developing and emphasizing the importance for the church to have The “Rule of Faith/Truth”. According to Irenaeus, the Rule of Faith is a summary of apostolic teaching that serves as a guide for interpreting Scripture and maintaining orthodox belief. This Rule of Faith includes several key elements:

This story guides right exegesis

This story is handed on by way of tradition

This story unifies the church

Therefore, the Gnostic reading of Scripture is invalid because it is not congruent with the Rule of Faith. In other words, Gnostics don’t have the right story guiding their reading of Scripture.

According to Irenaus, the Gospel is a seamlessly unified story of God forming humanity into the image of Christ, bringing us from infancy to maturity.

The unified story can be seen while the two hands of God, Word and Spirit, are forming humanity into image of God (from Gen. 1 until the consummation).

For Irenaeus, Humanity is originally good, free, and has capacity for growth. That means that the first humans were created innocent like toddlers and rebellious like teens. In this sense, the Old Testament is a period of education and growth, where God disciplines humanity like a loving parent. The New Testament is the period of maturity, where humanity is formed into the image of Christ through the incarnation, death, and resurrection of Jesus.

The Incarnation, then, sums up God’s plan (“recapitulates the divine economy”), i.e., Christ sums up or brings to completion the process of bringing humanity from infancy to maturity, from innocence to experience.

In Christ, God’s creation intent is fully revealed. We see the mature image of God, the destiny of all those who grow into the likeness of Christ through the work of the Spirit. “Christ became what we are that He might bring us to be even what He is,” i.e., the mature Adam, the image and likeness of God, and fully united to God.

Union or communion with God is fully restored in the consummation, when God’s intent at creation (Gen. 1:26) is fully realized.

This unified story contrasts with the modern Western tendency to divide human life into sacred and secular spheres. And also contrasts with the Creation-Fall-Redemption framework that sees human history as a tragic fall from grace that needs to be redeemed. It presents a more holistic and hopeful view of human history as a journey of growth and maturation under the guidance of God.

records.content:
Tertullian was an early Christian writer and theologian from Carthage in North Africa. He is often referred to as the “Father of Latin Christianity” due to his significant contributions to Christian theology and literature in the Latin language. He is very well known for his “What has Athens to do with Jerusalem?” argument, where he opposed the use of Greek philosophy in Christian theology.



Icon of Tertullian of Carthage

Tertullian also coined the term “Trinity” (from the latin trinitas) to describe the relationship between the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. He emphasized the unity of God while maintaining the distinctiveness of each person within the Godhead.

In his work “Against Praxeas,” Tertullian defends the doctrine of the Trinity against the heresy of 

Modalism, which denied the distinct persons of the Godhead. He argued that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three distinct persons who share one divine essence.

Tertullian and Cyprian develop a latin theology that will influence the Western Church for centuries to come while Origen and Clement of Alexandria will do the same for the Eastern Greek Church.

He was raised as a pagan but converted to Christianity when he was about forty, in Rome 

Gonzalez, 2010, pg. 88. Tertullian’s writings cover a wide range of topics, including apologetics, theology, ethics, and church discipline. He was a prolific writer, and his works had a lasting impact on the development of Christian doctrine and practice.

His anthithesis between Christianity and the pagan culture of his time set the tone for much of Western Christian thought in the centuries that followed.

Tertullian would become a 

Montanist later in life. He also advocated for private schools that teach Christian doctrine.

It is also in Tertullian writings that we have our first source of the practice of infant baptism in the early church.

Prominent Leaders in the Early Church

records.content:
Cyprian was a bishop of Carthage and an important early Christian writer and theologian. He is best known for his leadership during a time of persecution and his writings on church unity and discipline. He is considered the father of Ecclesiology in the Western Church.



Icon of St. Cyprian of Carthage

Cyprian is well known for his famous phrase “no one can have God as a father who does not have the Church as a mother.” He promotes a more pastoral and communal approach to Christianity compared to Tertullian’s more individualistic and rigorous stance.

Cyprian got converted to Christianity in his adulthood, 12 years before his martyrdon. He was so bright that they promoted him to bishop after 2 years of being a Christian.

During Diocletian’s persecution, Cyprian had to deal with the issue of Christians who had lapsed in their faith under persecution. He advocated for a balanced approach, allowing for the possibility of repentance and restoration to the church for those who had denied their faith but had shown genuine remorse. He also fled Carthage during the persecution, which led to some controversy regarding his leadership.

His teachings guide churches to believe you can be accepted in church again if you reject your faith under persecution but repent later. But that can only happen once. A second lapse is unforgivable.

He was later beheaded for his faith in 258 A.D. during the Valerian persecution.

The fourth aspect of the response to Gnosticism is the establishment of leadership structures within the early Christian communities. As the church grew and faced various challenges, it became necessary to have clear leadership to maintain doctrinal integrity and unity. The early church developed a hierarchical structure with bishops, presbyters (elders), and deacons.

Even though the roles were still developing, bishops were seen as the successors of the apostles and held the highest authority in the local church. They were responsible for teaching, governing, and safeguarding the faith. Presbyters assisted the bishops in pastoral care and administration, while deacons served in practical roles, such as caring for the poor and managing church resources.

These offices were not distinguished until Tertullian (ca. 160-225 A.D.) wrote about them in his work “On the Prescription of Heretics.” The development of this leadership structure helped to ensure that the teachings of the apostles were preserved and transmitted faithfully, providing stability and continuity for the early Christian communities.

There were mainly three cultural influences on the development of church leadership:

Social Influence: The “household of God” model was influenced by the Roman household structure, where the paterfamilias (head of the household) held authority over family members. This model was adapted to the church context, with bishops serving as spiritual heads of the Christian community.

Philosophical Influence: school leadership structures, such as those in Stoicism and Platonism, also influenced the church’s leadership model. These schools often had a hierarchical structure with a head teacher and assistants, which provided a framework for organizing church leadership.

Jewish Influence: The early Christian church inherited many leadership concepts from Jewish synagogue structures, where elders and teachers played significant roles in guiding the community.

Everyday Greco-Roman households consisted of approximately 50 persons from at least three generations, in addition to which there would be servants, slaves, tenants, clients, and others.

The household servants were called diakonoi (deacons). They were to obey the head of the household as they would obey God.

The head servant was called episkopos (bishop). He was in charge of the other servants and represented the master. Servants were to obey the head servant as if he was the master.

So, by analogy, a person in the church should obey the bishop/episkopos (the head servant) as one would obey God. A bishop is to be humble as a slave but he also speaks and acts on God’s behalf. He serves the members of the household, administering funds and meeting spiritual needs.

Many schools of philosophy co-existed with the Early Christianity in the Greco-Roman world. Regardless, Christianity claimed to be the true philosophy, and the church was God’s school.

Justin Martyr’s School

Justin Martyr (c. 100–165 AD) was an early Christian apologist and philosopher who established a Christian school in Rome.

Greco-Roman philosophical schools were communities intent on spiritual formation: A teacher and his disciples dialogued, ate together, and sometimes lived together. The goal of philosophical discourse was to persuade people to live in a certain way and to practice it.

Philosophy was not simply a way to think about life but a way of instilling attitudes and disciplined living; a disciple’s thinking and affections and actions needed to be converted. So disciples engaged in an inner battle between the old and the new life.

Christianity looked similar to these philosophical schools.

Leadership Terms from Philosophy

“Disciples” was Justin’s favorite term for Christians; he never speaks of episkopoi or presbyteroi. He describes the leader of the eucharist as a ‘presider’ (proestōs)—a term often used for the organizational head of philosophical schools.

In 

The Apostolic Constitutions, OT Israelite structures have parallels in the church. Three church offices were shaped by the duties of the Israelites.

➡️ The bishop is somewhat similar to the high priest,

➡️ presbyters to priests,

➡️ and deacons to Levites.

There also seemed to be a correlation between synagogue roles and developing church leadership roles.

The administrator of the church, an episkopos, acquired some functions of a Jewish archisynagogos (‘ruler/head/administrator of the synagogue’).

The diakonoi in the churches acquired some functions of the almoners and attendants in the Jewish synagogues.

Moreover, Christians, who, like Jews abstained from many normal civic functions, may have begun to organize themselves as a kind of distinct ‘ethnic community,’ which was neither Jew nor Gentile but claimed a ‘heavenly citizenship.’ The ‘seniors’ of this community were a kind of governing council which had the authority to appoint and advise the episkopos.

These are five key points about leadership in the early church before Christendom:

Priesthood of all believers.

Ministry which met community needs determined “offices”.

Practice, not merely a position.

Appointment to church office did not confer spiritual authority, but it recognized spiritual authority that was already evident.

Current theory for the first two centuries re. the “three offices”:

multiplicity of functions (readers, singers, porters, deaconesses, widows, virgins, orphans);

bishop dominant;

deacons perhaps more prominent ‘office’ than presbyters.

Leadership Views

Meaning

1. Priesthood of all believers

Every believer is a leader. Part of one’s baptism identity is being anointed as a priest who will serve the High Priest Jesus Christ.

2. Ministry which met community needs determined “offices”

As people exercised their gifts to meet needs, some of these ministries were communally recognized as official roles, e.g., prophets, healers, exorcists, widows, readers, virgins, subdeacons, hosts of agape meals, porters, grave diggers (fossores), ...

3. A practice, not merely a position

Ministry leadership, like the Christian life, was seen as a practice. E.g., Confessors: their faith and practice gave them the highest spiritual authority in their communities, not an “office” (position) as modern Christians think of “office.”

4. Appointment to church office did not confer spiritual authority, but it recognized spiritual authority that was already evident.

People who are exerting their gifts and have their spiritual authority are regocnized by receiving an office, and not the contrary.

Regarding point 5, in the first two centuries, we do not see a distinction between the roles of “clergy” and “laity.”  

Tertullian (early 3c) is the first Western theologian to make this distinction.

There was probably not a clear threefold ministry (bishop, elder, deacon) as we conceive it today: modern attempts to trace the development of offices in the church have often been “the investigator’s own denominational face at the bottom of a deep well” (Young 157).

In Acts and the Pastoral Epistles “elders” (presbyteroi) appears, but it is unclear what their relationship with an “overseer” or “bishop” (episkopos) is. They could be alternative terms for the same subject.

The multiplicity of functions (readers, singers, porters, deaconesses, widows, virgins, orphans) and the dominance of the bishop are more noticeable than a threefold office (

The Apostolic Constitutions).

episkopos and diakonoi

Bishops and deacons may have been the only appointed ‘officers’ of a congregation. The church was ‘God’s household’ (1 Tim 3:15): the episkopos was ‘God’s steward’ (Titus 1:7) and the diakonoi were the servants.

“presbyter”

An ambiguous term that suggested seniority: these senior citizens carried the community memory and therefore were responsible to teach the apostolic tradition. The episkopos turns to the senior members for advice, so they acted as an advisory council.

The Work of the Holy Spirit in Montanism

records.content:
Montanism was a charismatic movement that emerged in the late 2nd century AD, founded by Montanus, a Christian prophet from Phrygia (modern-day Turkey). Montanism emphasized the ongoing work of the Holy Spirit in the life of the church, particularly through prophecy and ecstatic experiences. Montanus, along with two prophetesses, Priscilla and Maximilla, claimed to receive direct revelations from the Holy Spirit, which they believed were a continuation of the apostolic age.

The two main characteristics of Montanism were its emphasis on new prophecy and its rigorous moral standards. Montanists believed that the Holy Spirit was actively guiding the church through new revelations, which sometimes challenged established church teachings and practices. They also advocated for a strict moral code, including asceticism, fasting, and celibacy.

Among the main montanist figures were:

Montanus: The founder of the movement, who claimed to be a prophet filled with the Holy Spirit.

Priscilla and Maximilla: Two prophetesses who played significant roles in the Montanist movement, also claiming to receive divine revelations.

Tertullian: An early Christian writer and theologian who later became a Montanist. He defended Montanism and its emphasis on the Holy Spirit in his writings.

Epiphanius of Salamis: A church father who wrote against Montanism, documenting its beliefs and practices in his work “Panarion.”

Apollonius of Ephesus: An early Christian writer who also opposed Montanism and provided valuable historical accounts of the movement.

The Canon withing the Canon

Each generatioon has a canon within the canon. We select specific texts from the Bible that speak to our context and situation. For the Montanists, the prophetic texts of the Old Testament (e.g., Joel, Ezekiel) and the Book of Revelation were particularly significant, as they emphasized the role of the Holy Spirit and the anticipation of Christ’s return.

Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–251 AD) was an early Christian theologian, scholar, and prolific writer. He is considered one of the most important figures in early Christian theology and biblical studies. Origen was born in Alexandria, Egypt, a major center of learning and culture in the ancient world. He later moved to Caesarea in Palestine, where he continued his scholarly work. He was a disciple of 

Clement of Alexandria and was deeply influenced by Platonic philosophy.

Origen is best known for his extensive writings on Christian theology, biblical exegesis, and philosophy. He produced a vast body of work, including commentaries on almost every book of the Bible, theological treatises, and apologetic writings defending Christianity against pagan and heretical critiques.

Origen’s Hexapla, a critical edition of the Old Testament in six parallel columns (Hebrew, Greek transliteration, and four Greek translations), was a monumental scholarly achievement that greatly influenced biblical studies.

Origen also developed the concept of the “spiritual interpretation” of Scripture, emphasizing the importance of understanding the deeper, allegorical meanings behind the literal text. This approach to biblical interpretation had a lasting impact on Christian theology and exegesis.

His ideas can be read at 

New Advent.

Origen’s theological stands on Scripture interpretation can be controversial. His analysis of allegorical meanings sometimes led him to conclusions that were at odds with orthodox Christian doctrine. For example, he proposed the pre-existence of souls and the eventual restoration of all beings, including the devil, which were later deemed heretical by the church. Still, his contributions to Christian thought and biblical scholarship remain significant. He is considered the first great biblical scholar of the early church.

His understanding that the Eternal Word (Logos) is incarnated in the text of the Scripture is a foundational idea for Christian theology. Origen believed that the Word of God is not only revealed through Jesus Christ but also through the sacred texts of the Bible. This concept underscores the importance of Scripture as a means of encountering and understanding God’s revelation.

Also, some principles of Origen’s hermeneutics (interpretation of Scripture) include:

Only those who believe that all Scripture is inspired by the Holy Spirit are able to interpret Scripture correctly.

An interpretation must be edifying to God’s people.

The Holy Spirit accommodates Scripture to the different capacities of people so that Scripture speaks to everyone. Although many people are only able to understand the literal meaning of Scripture, the Spirit both “edifies” them and “raises their apprehension” to a spiritual level through various means such as stumbling blocks.

Every part of Scripture is profitable.

The character of the interpreter is important. An interpreter should devote one’s whole soul to the words of God, be attentive, careful, diligent, reverent, of sound judgment, etc. The meaning of a text is hidden in proportion to the unworthiness of the interpreter.

Origen was martyred during the persecution of Christians under the Roman Emperor Decius around 251 AD. Despite the controversies surrounding some of his theological ideas, Origen’s legacy as a pioneering scholar and theologian continues to be recognized in Christian history.



Illustration of the torture of Origen of Alexandria by Jan Luyken, 1684. Martyrs Mirror, 1685. Origen sought martyrdom at an early age alongside his father, who was arrested by order of Lacto, governor of Egypt, because of his Christian faith and later beheaded. And if he did not do so, it was because his mother hid all his clothes, leaving Origen ashamed to go out like that. Later, he wrote his father a letter, known as “Exhortation to Martyrdom” where he encouraged him to go forward and confess Christ, without fear of leaving his family, because God would provide for the family. And God provided, for a rich woman took care of the widow and children, whose property, as the law required, had been confiscated.

This is a journal documenting my journey through the course “Story Of Christianity I” offered by Calvin Seminary. The course explores the history of Christianity from its origins to the medieval period, examining key events, figures, and theological developments.

This journal will include summaries of lectures, reflections on readings, and personal insights gained throughout the course. It aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the material covered and to deepen my understanding of the Christian faith and its historical context. The main goal is to inform myself and keep track of the knowledge acquired during this educational experience.

As we start studying church history, we may see our task as similar to that of an alien anthropologist trying to understand human culture. Imagine for a moment that you are an alien grad student in interplanetary religions, sent to Earth to study Christianity. You arrive on our planet with no prior knowledge of human history, culture, or religion. Your goal is to observe and analyze the practices, beliefs, and values of Christians throughout history. You are also short in funding, so you decide to focus on specific periods, coming back to your home planet to write reports after each visit.



Dr. Who and the Daleks (1965). A good representation of an alien anthropologist visiting Earth.

This exercise will help us understand the task of studying church history from a fresh perspective. By adopting the mindset of an alien anthropologist, we can approach church history with curiosity and openness, seeking to understand the “otherness” of past Christians.

By deriving our understanding of what are Christians from samples of different ages and places in church history, we can come to various conclusions about what Christianity is and how it has evolved over time. We can learn to appreciate the differences and similarities between our own context and that of past Christians. We can also see how the gospel has been communicated and lived out in different cultural settings.

After conducting our alien anthropological study of Christianity, we can ask ourselves:

What should the grad student in Earthly Christianity conclude about this strange religion?

Can we see how Christianity has been remarkably adaptive and resilient throughout history? It has been able to take root in diverse cultures and contexts, while still maintaining its core message and identity. This adaptability is a testament to the power of the Christian faith and its ability to speak to the human condition across time and space.

Can we see how Christians have often found themselves as “resident aliens” (

paroikoi) in their own cultures? They have had to navigate the tension between celebrating the culture and embodying alternatives to it. This tension has shaped the way Christians have lived out their faith throughout history.

Can we see how the study of church history can inform our own faith and practice today? By learning from the successes and failures of past Christians, we can gain insights into how to live out our faith in our own context.

The question of how to study church history is crucial for our understanding of the faith. It is not enough to simply know the events and figures of church history; we must also approach it with the right perspective and methodology. Some quotes presented during the lecture help us to reflect on this question:

In modernity, church history has often been taught not “in terms of the missionary advance in successive encounters of the gospel with different forms of human culture and society, but rather as a story of the doctrinal and other conflicts within the life of the church.” (L. Newbigin)

I wish someone had told me in seminary that the Christological and Trinitarian controversies of the second and third century were first and foremost issues of contextualization. (L. Newbigin)

We have to ask in all sincerity whether the study of the history of the church ought not to be completely redesigned. (David Bosch)

These quotes highlight the importance of approaching church history with a missional and contextual perspective. We should not just focus on doctrinal disputes but also on how the gospel has been communicated and lived out in different cultural settings.

To provide a tool for studying church history, Prof. Rylaarsdam introduced us the two principles for missional encounters with culture:

The indigenizing principle: Christianity enters a culture and finds customs that embody the way of Christ. Christians celebrate the culture. They are residents in it.

The pilgrim principle: Christianity enters a culture and finds ways in which the culture contradicts the way and teachings of Christ. Christians seek to embody alternatives. They are not fully at home; they are resident aliens (paroikoi) in it.

These two principles are constantly in tension with each other throughout church history. Christians have to navigate between celebrating the culture and embodying alternatives to it. And each generation has to discern how to live out these principles in their own context.

My notes on paroikoi

The connection of the pilgrim principle and the idea of Christians as “resident aliens” (paroikoi) reminded me of 1 Peter 2:11-12:

“Dear friends, I urge you, as foreigners and exiles (paroikoi), to abstain from sinful desires, which wage war against your soul. Live such good lives among the pagans that, though they accuse you of doing wrong, they may see your good deeds and glorify God on the day he visits us.”

The biggest challenge presented for us is to pursue “faithful contextualization rather than syncretistic accommodation”.

Since the Gospel is translatable by its very nature, it can take on many cultural forms. In that translation the Gospel both affirms the creational good and judges the idolatrous twisting of all cultural forms. (Mike Goheen)

A framework for studying church history faithfully involves asking in each historical context:

What’s my context?

What’s the gospel in this context?

What’s the mission of God’s people in this context?

As a ministry leader, how can I equip people for mission in this context?

These questions help us to approach church history with a missional and contextual perspective, allowing us to learn from the past and apply those lessons to our own lives and ministries today. And they will be part of the following discussions throughout the course.

The main question of this topic will be: Why study the history of Christianity? Or as stated by Prof. Rylaarsdam, “What difference does it make to know church history?”

It is quite common for seminary students to question the relevance of church history for their ministry. Some may see it as a mere academic exercise, while others may view it as a distraction from more practical concerns. However, studying church history is essential for several reasons, which will be explored in this topic.



St Peter Preaching in the Presence of St Mark. Fra Angelico, c. 1440-41. 

Source

To summarize, here are some of the key reasons to study church history:

To understand our identity as Christians: Church history helps us to see how our faith has been shaped and formed over the centuries. It reminds us that we are part of a larger story, a story that goes back to the early church and continues to this day.

To learn from the past: By studying church history, we can learn from the successes and failures of those who came before us. We can see how they navigated challenges and controversies, and we can apply those lessons to our own lives and ministries.

To appreciate the diversity of the Christian tradition: Church history reveals the rich diversity of the Christian tradition. It shows us how different cultures and contexts have shaped the way we understand and practice our faith.

To deepen our faith: Studying church history can deepen our faith by helping us to see the faithfulness of God throughout the ages. It reminds us that we are part of a larger story of God’s work in the world.

Church history forms Christians for a missional encounter with culture as we observe how the church in the past did that. It is not just an academic exercise but a practical one that equips us to live out our faith in the world today.

The term “martyr” comes from the Greek word “μάρτυς” (mártus), which means “witness.”

In the context of early Christianity, martyrs were individuals who bore witness to their faith in Jesus Christ, even to the point of death. The early Christian martyrs were often persecuted by the Roman authorities for their refusal to renounce their faith and participate in the state-sanctioned religious practices, which were seen as a threat to the unity and stability of the Roman Empire.

The stories of the martyrs were highly influential in shaping the identity and theology of the early Christian church. Their courage and steadfastness in the face of persecution served as powerful examples of faith and devotion, inspiring other Christians to remain faithful even in difficult circumstances. The martyrdom of early Christians was often seen as a form of participation in the suffering and death of Christ, and it was believed that those who died for their faith would receive special rewards in the afterlife.

records.content:
A great deal of Scriptural texts were used by the early Christians to encourage and strengthen the faith of the martyrs. Some of the key passages that were particularly meaningful to them include:

Mark 8:34-35: “Then he called the crowd to him along with his disciples and said: ‘Whoever wants to be my disciple must deny themselves and take up their cross and follow me. For whoever wants to save their life will lose it, but whoever loses their life for me and for the gospel will save it.’”

Matthew 5:10-12: “Blessed are those who are persecuted because of righteousness, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are you when people insult you, persecute you and falsely say all kinds of evil against you because of me. Rejoice and be glad, because great is your reward in heaven, for in the same way they persecuted the prophets who were before you.”

Philippians 1:21: “For to me, to live is Christ and to die is gain.”

2 Corinthians 12:10: “That is why, for Christ’s sake, I delight in weaknesses, in insults, in hardships, in persecutions, in difficulties. For when I am weak, then I am strong.”

2 Timothy 4:6-8: “For I am already being poured out like a drink offering, and the time for my departure is near. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith. Now there is in store for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous Judge, will award to me on that day—and not only to me, but also to all who have longed for his appearing.”

Revelation 14:13: “Then I heard a voice from heaven say, ‘Write this: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on.’ ‘Yes,’ says the Spirit, ‘they will rest from their labor, for their deeds will follow them.’”

Romans 8:35-39: “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall trouble or hardship or persecution or famine or nakedness or danger or sword? As it is written: ‘For your sake we face death all day long; we are considered as sheep to be slaughtered.’ No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us. For I am convinced that neither death nor life, neither angels nor demons, neither the present nor the future, nor any powers, neither height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord.”

Revelation 2:10: “Do not be afraid of what you are about to suffer. I tell you, the devil will put some of you in prison to test you, and you will suffer persecution for ten days. Be faithful, even to the point of death, and I will give you life as your victor’s crown.”

It is important to remember that Stephen’s martyrdom and Jesus’ crucifixion set models for the early Christian martyrs. Stephen, as the first Christian martyr, exemplified forgiveness and faithfulness even in the face of death (Acts 7:54-60). Jesus’ own suffering and death on the cross served as the ultimate example of sacrificial love and obedience to God’s will (Philippians 2:5-11). These examples provided a theological framework for understanding martyrdom as a participation in Christ’s own suffering and a witness to the truth of the gospel.

The martyrs of the early church would see themselves as 

Paroikoi (resident aliens), a very important concept, as they saw themselves as pilgrims in this world, not fully at home, and looking forward to their true home in heaven.

Later, when Christianity become legal in the Roman Empire, the pilgrim principle will be co-existing with the indigenizing principle, which will create tensions in the church.

The paradox of the Christian life is a very good place to reflect upon the experience of the martyrs. Christians are called to live in the world but not be of the world (John 17:14-16). They are to be in the world as witnesses to the truth of the gospel, but they are also called to embody an alternative way of life that reflects the values of the kingdom of God.

The concept of dual citizenship captures this paradox, as Christians are citizens of both the earthly kingdom and the heavenly kingdom. This dual citizenship creates a tension between the demands of the world and the demands of faith, which the martyrs experienced in a profound way.

Diognetus Epistle provides a beautiful description of the Christian identity as resident aliens:

“They live in their respective countries, but only as resident aliens 

paroikoi; they participate in all things as citizens, and they endure all things as foreigners [...] They marry like everyone else and have children, but they do not expose them once they are born. They share their meals but not their sexual partners [...] To put the matter simply, what the soul is in the body, this is what Christians are in the world.”

Epistle to Diognetus (2c)

On Diognetus Epistle

There was certainly an increase in persecutions during the reign of Emperor Nero (54-68 AD), particularly after the Great Fire of Rome in 64 AD, which Nero blamed on the Christians. This led to widespread persecution and martyrdom of Christians in Rome. 

Gonzalez, 2010 will again help us understand that Christians were easy targets for Nero, as they were a marginalized and misunderstood group in Roman society. They were often accused of atheism (due to their refusal to worship the Roman gods) and of engaging in secret and subversive activities. This made them vulnerable to persecution, especially during times of crisis or unrest.



Nero walks on Rome’s cinders, by Karl Theodor von Piloty, 1861, Hungarian National Gallery

On Nero’s Persecution

Interestingly, there are no records of empire-wide persecutions of Christians until the reign of Emperor Decius (249-251 AD). Decius issued an edict in 250 AD that required all citizens of the empire to perform a sacrifice to the Roman gods and the emperor, which Christians refused to do. This led to a widespread persecution of Christians throughout the empire, with many being arrested, tortured, and executed for their faith.
